A ring of cork fits into this, in which is placed a glass or stoneware stopper. The principle of stopping or closing the orifices of bottles jor other vessels with cork is well understood. Nevertheless, the present method of its application is open to many objec- tions, the consideration of which will serve to illus- trate the superior advantage that the new invention and application of hollow corks present; and as a superior effect is produced, and no new material used, their introduction is not calculated to excite any opposition on the part of those who are in favour of the present or solid corks. The application of hollow corks in reality improves ?? the principle of solid corks, and it is hoped that their superiority will remove the disadvantages which have hitherto ex- isted. The Royal Patent Decorative Glass Works of Southwark Bridge-road show some fine specimens of their new vitrified lace-pattern glass. The process and the effects produced are entirelynovel. Perfect representations of net or muslin curtains, with embroidered borders (correct in every detail), and every description of lace pattern, may be produced by this very ingenious process. The material used for the matt or groundwork is different from that usually employed; it is more even in surface, and will retain its purity of colour without being affected by exposure to the atmosphere, and it has a semi- transparent appearance, not found in any work of a similar character. For internal embellishments it appears to possess decided advantages over other descriptions of white ornamented glass. It has the same appearance from both sides, does not require the aid of a light behind to show the design, and the ornament stands out in strong relief when viewed by artificial light. On Monday, thie 4th inst., the total nmmber of visitors was 62,631, and tho total receipts, 3,028 18s. Yesterday the number of visitors was 58,634, and the receipts 2,835 9s., including 5 10s. for season tickets. This falling-off is very slight, considering 1he enormous numbers who have had an opportunity of visiting the building since its inauguration. ''iie diminution is certainly rather desirable than otherwise, when. it is considered how the denser concourses of a few wecks back, reaching sometimes to between seventy and eighty thousand, precluded a satisfactory examination of the uost interesting objects. The weather yesterday was delightful, and thousands of all classes took advantago of the excursion trains which were started early in the morning from all parts of the country, to accommodate visitors to the Crystal Palace. No fewer than between 18,000 and 19,000 poured in nt the doors during the first hour after they had been opened, and botween eleven and twelve o'clock the crowds admitted had risen to 37,312. Between twelve and one, 9,516 more entered ; between one and two, 5,276; between two and three, 3,080 - between three and four, 1,990 ; between four and five, 1,100; making thte total up to five o'clock, 58,274. We mentioned yesterday that fresh importations of arti- cles for exhibition had arrived on Saturday from the United States. To-day they were in the course of being unpacked. We are informed that they consist of eight or nine more carriages, some five-and-twenty additional cases of agricul- tural implements, such as ploughs, hoes, harrows, rakes, and spades, besides several specimens of cotton-gins which are used in the States for extractiig the seed from the cotton plant. We understand that several of the American light 4 ploughs now exhibited are rapidly getting into great favourI ir, this country. The following is a copy of the letter addressed by the Mlarquis of Normauby to Earl Grauville, in re- ply to the request of his lordship, on behalf of the visitors to Paris, to express to the President of the Republic and the Prefect of the Seine the grateful acknowledgments of the kind and cordial reception which they had met at the hands of all classes in Paris " Paris, August 7. My dear Granville-Pray assure the gentlemen who have signed the letter which you have committed to my charge that I will take the earliest opportunity to communicate the sentiments expressed ir. that paper to the President of the Itepublic and the Prefect of the Seine. " It is my intention to write officially to the Minister for Foreign Affairs on the subject, and also to repeat verbally, beth to the President and to the Prefect of the Seine these expressions of gratitude on the part of the commissioners, jurors, and others connected with the Exhibition. " I em convinced that the Prince, and all the members of his Government, will receive with much satisfaction the assurances that their cordial hospitality has been duly ap- preciated by those to whom it was freely offered, and it is a matter of gratification to me, as the representative of my Sovereign, to be the medium of naling known to the Government to which I am accredited such a declaration on the part of my countrymen. " Having, during the last five years of uninterrupted re- sidence in ithis country, laboured incessantly, under varied circumstances, to promnote a kindly feeling between these two great neighboring people, I receive from you with peculiar pleasure this testinsony of the first beneficial result of the Great Exhibition, in itself so wsell calculated to pro- mote the development of mutual goodwill amongst nations. " The city of Paris on this occasion has displayed no idle or unmeaning hospitality, if frem a survey of its municipal constitution we can gather a full impression of the necessity which exists for reforming that of London, and if from the examination of its magnificent public ?? and institu- norms, founded and liberally supported by Government for the free use of an intelligent people, we can borrow ideas to be realised hereafter, whereby our industrial energies may be directed by the rules of good taste, and a more artistic spirit be harmoniously combined withl the strong utilita- rian tendencies of our manufactures." These very curious and uncommon specimens of taxidermy in fuln and taxidermy in earnest, form undoubtedly -in a small way-one of the most remarkable features of the Exhibition. Thle expression managed to be por- trayed on the faces of the aninmals is semi-human, and yet there is nothing in the slightest degree re- volting or forbidding in the representation. Mon- keys and apes, whose faces resemble in some degree those of men, wye are accustomed to consider as hideously ugly crea. tures, and, indeed, as something degrading to contemplate. Not so the " Comical Creatures from Wurtemburg." The fox, although in look infinitely more sage and more sly thea many of his hunian admirers, is a fox still. The rabbit, too, although his honest hairy face may be a thought less stupid than some whiel stare into it, is also a rabbit still. The animals borrow exaggerated expression, without losing their brute looks; and the r1tioalae of the irresistible risibility which they excite, is the wondrous union of brute face with human expression. InI a previous article upon the Exhibition we alluded to the tendency of the German mind to construct legends of which the loner asnimals were the personages and d'assntis pcrsoltte. Thle qualities of the population of a quiet High.Dutch. village were transferred to hares, weasels, bears, rabbits, foxes, and wolves-with, perhaps, here and there a supernatural old griffiu or dragon; arud the little scandals and incidents of botiseliold life were made over from the chimney-corner and the garden to the forest and the field. Of the many German stories of this class, that of " Leynard the Fox" is the oldest aiid the most famous. Carlyle says, " Among, the people it was long a house-book and universal best companion it lias been lectured on in universities-quoted in impe- rial council halls-it lay on the toilets of princes- and was thumbed to pieces ois the bench of the artLizan. We hear of grave men ranking it next to their Bible." With this rather extravagant degree of admiration we certainly do not coincide. " Reynard the Fox " is a tolerably good piece of well-intentioned whimsicality ; but " Jack the Giant Killer," or " Puss in Boots," is worth a dozen of it. Goethe, however, tolk the story as the subject of a great poem-a fact Wihich, to some extent, we fear, proves that Goethe, in vulgar phrase, must have been very " hard lip " for subjects; amid Kaultachi, the weell-hnown German painter, adorned this poem with a series of thoroughly characteristic pictures, from wihic Herrmannii PlaqUet, the constrictor of the " Comical Creatures from Wtirtemburg," has copied no less titan six of his figures. The other groups of aanimals are what we may call fancy sketches in fur, and are just as oddly hiuman as the copies from KRaulbacli. The stall in which these odd preparations are placed is one of the issost crowded points of the Exhibition, and iithiing can be more genuine thaou the admiration, or more hearty than the laughter, with wvhichi thie civilleed anin.als are greeted. The notion of preserving their forms and expres- sions by means of the unfailing daguerreotype-of multiply- ing the impressions by the help of careful and minuto sood- en3gravings-of expounding and setting forth the legend of " Reyuiard the Fox" by a pleasantly executed translation-of giving a coherence and a literary consistency to the other groups by means of uinpretendilmg little stories invented for thie nonce-the notion, in fine, of embodying all these reminiscences of the Exhibition, and of German fancy and quainit imvention, in a pretty little folio- was an exceedingly happy one, and one which, we doubt not, will be eminently successful. Mr. Bogue, of Fleet-street, has ushered into the world this literary me- mento of the " Comical Creatures from Wurtemburg." The tales other than that of Reynard aspire to little literary nmerit, but they ?? together the subjects of the plates aid give to each a significance and a point which will be readily associated with the piquant expressions of the ani- mals. The drawings are careful and clever, and convey a very correct representation of the original creatures, with all, or nearly all, their subtlety of expression and aspect. The capitsl fatuity of the rabbits and hares, the delight- ful scoundrelism of the fox, the culning shrewdness of the martens and weasels, the hoyden visages of the kittens, and the cool, slippery demeanour of the frogs, are all capitally given. The book is a clever and a pleasant memento of the Exhibition. It may lie on the drawing-roomn table, or be thumbed in the nursery; and in the latter case we have little doubt that minany an urchin still in petticoats will in future years associate his most vivid recollection of the Great Exhi- bitioim of 1851 with Mr-. THE ORIGIN AND HISTORY OF THE GREAT EXHIBITION. lOn Thursday, the great event took place which has for the last sixteen months occupiedin a greater or a lesser degree the attention of the people, not only of this country, but of the civilized world. In the midst of royalty and rank, and all that is great and illustrious in the land, the opening of the Exhibition took place. People of all realms and of all climes will, during the coming months, view with wonder and delight, and with profit and advantage, the rich treasures from the bowels of the earth, the mighty deep, and the realms of animal and vegetable creation, together with the display of mechanical invention, and the productions of industry and art which, collected from the four quarters of the globe, will be there spread out before them. "In other countries and other climes," said the great statesman whose loss the nation yet deplores, "splendid spectacles have been provided for the gratification of the people. There still remain the ruins of ancient edifices, almost uninjured by time, where, for the gratification of the people, showy and costly spectacles were provided. On a Roman holiday hecatombs of wild beasts were slain, and sanguinary conflicts took place of man against man. We propose, however, to gratify the people by other agencies mote in harmony with our civilisation and Christianity—to teach them gratitude to the Almighty Creator by exhibiting the wonderful contrivances of nature for the happiness of man, and to draw closer the bonds of amity and general intercourse, by the honest rivalry of industry and skill." The great success of the last French Exposition caused several representations to be made to members of the Cabin( t of this country, of the benefit which a similar exhibition would be likely to confer on the industry of the United Kingdom, and efbrts were made to obtain the assistance of the G ivernment, but with no apparent results, and no hapes were held out that the Government would be induced to undertake any pecuniary liabilities in the promotion of such an exhibi ion. Even so late as the year 1848, a proposal to establish a self-sudporting exhitoi , ion of Btilish industry, to be controlled by a royal commission, was submitted to his Royal Highness Ptince Albert, and by him laid before the Government, which still hesitated to take up the subject; and it became, therefore, evident to those parties who were most desirous of wimessing the establishment of a national exhibition, that if such an event should ever take place, it would have to be carried out independently of any assistance of that character. The Society of Arts, however, appear steadily to have kept the idea in sight. To assist in carrying out its intention of holding a National Exhibition in the year 1851, the council of the society caused a report on the French Exposition, held in 1849, to be made for them by Mr. D. Wyatt; a petition was also presented by the council to the House of Commons, praying that the society might have the use of some public building for the Exhibition of 1851. At the close of the session of 1849, Prince Albert, who, as president of the Society of Arts, had fully concurred in all the steps taken upon this subject by the society, took the matter more immediately under his own personal superintendence. The enlarged and liberal views which his Royal Highness took upon the subject could not, however, be confined within the compara ively small area of an Exhibition of British Industry. In framing the general outlines of the undertaking, his Royal Highness, at a meeting of several members of the Society of Arts, held at Buckingham Palace on the 30th of June, proposed that the Exhibition should be divided into four sections—the first being raw materials and produce, illustrative of the natural productions on which human industry is employed. The second, machinery for.agriculturing, manufacturing, engineering, and other purposes, and mechanical inventions—idustrative of the agents which human ingenuity brings to bear upon the products of nature. The third, manutactures—illustrative of the result produced by the operation of human industry upon natural produce. And the fon th, sculpture, models, and the plastic arts generally—illustrative of the tastes and skill displayed in such applications. At this meeting also, His Royal Highness pointed out the vacant ground in Hydepark, on the south side, parallel with and between the Kensington-drive and the ride commonly called Rotten-row, as affording advantages whtch few other places might be found to possess, and for which site application could be made to the Crown. It was also decided that a Royal Commission should be issued, of which his Royal Highness Prince Albert should be the head. At this stage of the proceedings it was considered advisable, by the Council of the Society of Arts, to enter at once into pecUniary arrangements calculated to insure the carrying out of the proposed plan. After considerable negociation with several builders and contractors, an agreement was entered into between the Socie, y of Arts and Messrs. Munday, by which the latter undertook to deposit £20,000 as a prize fund, to erect a suitable building, to find offices, to advance the money requisite for all preliminary expenses, and to tade the whole risk of loss on certain conditions. It was proposed thA the receipts arising from the Exhibition should be dealt with as follows :—The £20,000 prize fund, the cost of the building, and the five per cent. on all advances, were to be repa d in the first instance ; the residue was then to be devided into three equal parts; one part was to be paid at onceto the Society of Arts as a fund for future exhibitions: out of the other two parts, all other incidental costs, such as those of general management, preliminary expenses, &c., were to be paid ; and the residue, if any, was to be the remuneration of the contractors for their outlay, trouble, and risk. Subsequently the contractors agreed that instead of this division they would be content to receive such part of the surplus, if any, as, after payment of all expenses, might be awarded to them by arbitration. This, however, was subsequently put aside, and £23,000, with the interest which had accrued, was paid to them as compensation. BOBBIN-NET MACHINERY. -Nottingham, long celebrated for her machine-made lace, has, on this occasion, furnished indubitable proofs that her manufacturers and artisans have been progressing in the same ratio as those in most other branches of industry, during the last half- century. Fifty years ago, lace made by mashinery was mostly from the point-net and warp-machines (both modifications of the original stocking-frame); since that period, there have been incredible sums of money ex- pended, many valuable lives sacrificed by intense study, hundreds of patents taken out, and nearly as many differ- ently-constructed machines built for the production of plain and ornamental lace of every description. It has been matter of astonishment to see how quickly one inventor has succeeded another, and by simplifying or modifying his machines rendered useless those of his predecessor. It may be stated, that in none of the textile fabrics have there been so many combinations of ma- chinery used to effect the purpose as in the making of lace, commencing with the stocking-frame, to which was added a Tickler machine, then the point-net machine, warp machine, Mechlin plait machine, and many others. All of these (except the warp machine,) disappeared for the purpose of making lace when the bobbin-net machine was introduced, and its capabilities for making both plain and ornamnental lace became developed. The bobbin-net ma- chine is so called from the thread that makes the lace being partly supplied from bobbins, and partly from a warp, the bobbins being made to pass from front to back, and back to front, while a lateral motion is imparted to the warp threads, thus causing one series of threads to warp round the other. We to-day continue our descriptions of the articles exhibited in the class devoted to Furniture Decorations, &c., selecting for our present notice the various specimens of oil-cloths exhibited; and we also give some additional information with respect to the beautiful specimens of Statuary Porcelain exhibited, and the process of their manufacture. FURNITURE DECORATIONS.-No. VII. * FLOOR CLOTHS. The floor cloths exhibited are more than creditable to the producers, and are well calculated to convey a most favourable impression of the taste and skill displayed in this branch of manufacture, and which is one of considerable importance in the metropolis. We believe that a century has scarcely elapsed since the first patent was taken out for making floor cloths by block printing, a process identical with that used for the printing of cotton goods and the manufacture of paper-hangings. This patent was obtained by Mr. Smith, the founder of the firm of Smith and Baber, the extensive manufacturers at Knightsbridge, and the process has entirely superseded the old method of producing floor cloths by plates and stencilling. Floorcloths being intended generally for situations where carpets would not be appropriate--where marble or stone floors, cane and India matting, or parquetrie, might be expected to be met with--the most appropriate class of designs are those of a simple and geometric character. The quality of a floor cloth depends even more upon the purity of the paint used than upon the quality of the canvas painted upon. Unadulterated white lead will produce a cloth that will endure almost as long as the stone of which it may possibly form the cover; and the firmness or stiffness of a floor cloth gives no idea of its quality, as a coating of strong size on the canvas previously to commencing to paint it will produce all that may be wished in this respect, and much more than can be produced by any number of coats of the purest paint. The canvass on which these cloths are produced is manufactured almost exclusively at Dundee; and as it is made eight yards wide, it allows the manufacturer to make his cloths suitable for all probable purposes without the necessity of seaming. One of the finest of this class of productions is unquestionably the one shown by Messrs. Smith and Baber. This cloth is suspended in the carriage riage court at the north-west corner of the Exhibition, and is a remarkable specimen of design, composed principally from forms given by Mr. Lyson, in his admirable work on the Roman villa found in the latter part of the last century near Goodchester. The general arrangement in plan consists of a circular centre formed by guilloches inlaid with tesser, a peculiar vase-like ornament at the corner, a guilloche band, a fine rich outer border of octangular figures, and patter finished by an outer band of well-drawn fret ornament. This design has the merit of being admirably adapted for the purpose of a floor cloth; the colouring, too, exemplifies a fine taste, and as a whole we regard it as an unexceptionably beautiful production. Messrs. Hlare and Co., of Bristol, are the exhi- bitors of some large and varied productions that occupy a prominent position in the gallery north- west of the transept. In these we have every variety of ?? and Roman pavements, carpet patterns, well-drawn parqueterie designs and imitations of inlaid flooring ; also some nicely designed Alhambra scroll ornament. It is evident that no one of these productions is intended to be viewed as a whole in respect to design; and, as an arrangement of patterns, we think that consider- able skill is shown in the combination, whilst many of them are such as will rank among the best of this class of productions. We have looked with considerable interest to the' attempt to manufacture floorcloth with white zinc paint, the result being one of much moment to the artizans engaged in this work, as the material now in use is highly injurious to health, and no doubt l seriously affects the duration of life of the persons so employed. We regret to state, as far as our observations have extended, that the attempts to make floorcloths of spelter paint have failed- first, on account of the appearance the cloth presents, and secondly on account of increased cost in production. A cloth printed with the ma- terial in question has none of the fine glossy surface shown by the cloths made of the ordinary white lead, but looks as if the paint had been mixed with turpentine only, having the appearance of being what painters denominate " flatted"-and that, too when a much greater relative quantity of oil had been used. We have been informed, however, that this cloth presented the appearance of being " seasoned" at the end of four months, quite as much so as the ordinary cloth does at the end of seven or eight. But if even the matter of appear- ance-for we cannot speak as to wear, as yet-did I not militate against the use of zinc paint for floor- cloths, we fear that the increased cost of produc- tion would be fatal; for not only is the zinc paint about 8 per cent. dearer, but it requires a much larger quantity of oil in the working. We state this as being the result of experiments made on a large scale; but we still hope that attention to the manufacture of the paint in question may ulti- mately enable the painter of floorcloths to avail himself of the benefits that arise to health in using it, as compared with the ordinary white lead. STATUAUY PORCELAIN. The large amount of attention which the specimens formed I of this very beautiful material attract in the collection of Mr. Alderman Copeland, .P., Mr. Hinton, and Messrs. Rose and Co., and other exhibitors-as well as the wide i field which it throws open for the cultivation of a love of the fine arts among those to whom the productions of the sculptor are inaccessible-induces us to give sorme additional information with respect to this class of articles. The substance known as statuary porcelain was first in- vented by Mr. Thomas Battam, the manager of Mr. Alderma i Copeland's extensive ceramic manafartory at Stoke-upon- i Trent, and was prominently brought under public notice by the Art Union of London, which gave as one of its prizes a copy of Gibson's Narcissus, formed of this material. The principal ingredients in this composition are kaolin, felspar, and silica, ground and mixed together in the ordi- nary method adopted in the general processes of this manu- facture. It is prepared for the use of the figure makers in a state technically called " slip," about the consistency of I thick cream. In this state it is poured into the different moulds forming the sub-divisions of the figure or group, i which, being made of gypsum (plaster of Paris), rapidly ab- I sorb a portion of the moisture, and reduce the coating im- i mediately next the mould to a semi-clay state, of a suffi. cient thickness for the " cast," when the superfluous " slip" is them poured back from the moulds. This cast remains in the mould for some time at a high temperature, which, by causing still further evaporation, gradually reduces the " slip"I to a state of " clay" sufficiently firm to support its own weight alien relieved from the moulds, and to bear the necessary pressure of the handling without injury. The various parts (and in some groups there are as many as fifty) are then deli- vered from the moulds. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. We give to-day our concluding critical and descriptive notices of works of art, industry, and science which but a few days since were exa- mined with interest and admiration by hundreds of thousands, but the majority of which are now rapidly being distributed among those by whom they were contributed. The present notice is the last of our series of articles upon those productions more especially adapted for ecclesiastical uses. and orna- ments. ECCLESIASTICAL DEPARTMENT OF THE EXHIIBITION.-No. XV.* CONCLUDING PAPER. Having noticed in former papers, under appro- priate heads, the principal contents of the Exhibi- tion sharing aln ecclesiastical character, we have, in conclusion, put together, almost at random, a few additional remarks on topics which have not fallen into the general divisions of the subject. Among the many gratifying retrospects of the Exhibition, we may reckon the evident growing predilection for the use of various granites and marbles, as materials for architectural construc- tion and decoration. Some very beautiful specimens of madrepore and deep chocolate-coloured marble, sent from Mr. Charnpernowne's quarries at Dart- ington, near Totnes, may be especially noticed. But we did not observe any such complete col- lection of the products of our own quarries as was exhibited of all the marbles from the Vosges chain, and again as the interesting spe- cimens of the marbles of the Pyrenees contributed by M. Derville and Co., of Marseilles. From Spain aud Portugal also there were complete col- lections of the marbles of those countries. The marbles of Italy were illustrated in the exquisite mosaics froni Rome and Florence. Among the building materials from our own islands, we noticed the successful application of slate, in unusually thick slabs, to subh purposes as ridge-crests. We were glad to observe a more extensive use of our native marbles in domestic furniture. The Russian specimens of veneering in malachite formed a point of great attraction in the Exhibi- tiou; The piecing together of this very beautiful material is doubtless a not improper treatment of such a substance; but we doubt if it can be cousi- dered in conformity with principles of reality thus to use this ingenious veneering, not merely as a sub- sidiary ornament, but as if mnalachite were itself capable of being cut into huge slabs and used in construction. We should coufine our praise of NM. Demidoff's malachite to the exceeding skill shown in the comlbinatiou of its fragments ; fur not only were soile of its applications most unsuitable, but the style of ornament in which it was worked up, and especially in the concomitant metal work, was of a very corrupt character. It is singular that in the sofa in the Indian Court, formed of Rajpootana marble, this beautiful material was not used in a proper constructional manner, although reality is almost a universal principle in the art of Oriental civilization. The ivory chair, on the contrary, which was placed under the tent in the middle of the Court, was constrncted on a much better principle. Tile horn furniture of Hamburg, whatever may be thought of the propriety or good taste of so using such materials, deserves at least the credit of strict reality of construction. It may be reckoned a step in the right direction that the use of wood, inlaid in patterns, is be- ginning, it would seem, to be revived for purposes of flooring. Modern floors, for the most part, abso- lutely require their ugliness to be concealed by car- pets ; and the custom has been to paint a deal floor oak-colour, if any part is exposed beyond the extent of the carpet on stairs or in dining rooms. Mr. Leistler exhibited an excellent specimen of inlaid flooring in his Austrian suite of rooms: and, as applied also to ecclesiastical or semi-ecclesiastical purposes, the aid of machinery has been very ser- viceably employed by Mr. Pratt, of New Bond- street, iu reducing the price of the " inlaid parquet flooring," of which lie exhibited some specimens. But while on the one hand marbles and other real materials are more freely used than heretofore, on the other bland, we are sorry to say, imitation sub- stances appear to be increasing in number if not in favour. Messrs. Austen and Seeley exhibited a fountain made of their artificial stone, which how- ever (we should think) must have disenchanted any possible admirers of that substance, since under the influence of its spray, it never looked otherwise than damp and green and pervious to water. Equally unsuccessful was a Corinthian capital, in the Enig- lish nave, made of papicr-?naeh6. Its exhibitor, Mr. Bielfield, furnished also numerous specimens of both gothic and classical architectural mouldings and oruaments in the same material. Ill carto m-pierre, M. Mayer, of Munich, exhibited a rather vulgarly designed statue of the Blessed Virgin and Child. Being coloured, the actual ma- terial could never have been guessed. We may mention, also, that the English part of the Exhibition contained all sorts of architectural mouldings, flowers, pendants, &c., made of gutta percha; while another person produced the same in patent stone, or even in leather, under the name of " rolievo leather tapestry." Messrs. Willock and Co., of Manchester, besides the hideous Lever Bridge church, displayed capitals, poppy-heads, &c., in terra cotta. Mr. Denis, of London, imi- tated marble very skilfully in his scagliola. Indeed there appears to be no end of artificial building mia- terials; and the main object of nearly all the ex- hibitors of this kind seems to be to counterfeit in some sham substance the appearance, without the properties, of something else. But with all this, the tide is undoubtedly setting in favour of the principle of reality in construction and ornament. Even railway carriages are now made to depend for decoration on the grain of the wood of which they are constructed, which is brought out and heightened by varnish, instead of being concealed under thick coats of paint. The Great Northern Railway Company was the first, we believe, to iitroduce this at once rational and economical innovation ; but the example has been widely followed by other companies. The Exhibi- tion building contained a beautiful railway carriage by Mr. Williams so finished; and nothing excited more general commendation, we believe, in the carriage department, than a dog-cart which had neither colour nor ornament beyond the fihe grain of the highly-polished and varnished wood of which it was built. Similarly in the department of North Germany, there was a very conspicuous field-piece, mounted on a beau- tifully framed and polished gun-carriage, no paint at all being used, either on the carriage itself, or on the ramrod and other accessories. It should be added, that we were informed by a practical authority that carriages generally would be iore durable if varnished only, and not painted ; and in churches especially it is well known that the dry- rot extends its ravages far more widely and irreme- diably under the deceitful exterior of a coat of paint, than when the woodwork is exposed in its proper substance to the free air. We do indeed hope that we may have seen the beginning of the end of that nearly universal but absurd fashion of " graining"-that is, the clumsy imitation in paint of the grain of oak, and indeed of imitating generally the more expensive and beautiful woods on some cheap and common material. Few people know how really beautiful is the grain even of the common deal- timber, when highly varnished, without, however, any colouring matter being introduced. The design of organ-cases, and the arrangement of their pipes, present a great field for the revival of more true and real principles of construction. The organs in the Exhibition were generally, in this respect, inferior ; but we noticed a chamber- organ, by M. Alexandre, of Paris, in which the pipes were exposed and made part of the design, instead of being concealed behind a sham case. No colour was employed in this example. We must ex- press both surprise and regret that. Mr. Pugin did not display an organ case in his Medi.Tval Court. The organ erected by him in Jesus College Chapel, Cambridge, is so original in conception and so grace- ful in its colouring that we are sure he could have produced something which would have surpassed his other church furniture, had he but included an organ in his (so-called) medimeval display. Mr. Cleaver has exaggerated all the exam- ples he gave of ecclesiastical binding; and Mr. Barritt, of Fleet-street, who described himself as an " ecclesiastical binder," has not escaped the same fault, besides showing much general coarseness and absence of good taste in the ornamentation he has chosen. We shall not notice polychromatic printing, except to call attention to two very splendid works -of the highest ecclesiastical and antiquarian interest-of which specimens were exhibited in the French and Russian departments. The former is the series of copies of illuminated maniscriptsi of the Greek, Roman, Carlovingian, Capetian, and German styles, published by the French Govern- , meat under the direction of Comte Auguste de Bastard. The other is the sumptuous collection of the ecolesiological antiquities of the Oriental Church in Course of publication by the Russian Government. We have thus completed our task of reviewing I the general contents of the Exhibition, with the intention of noticing primarily the works of art and industry intended for ecclesiastical purposes ; and, secondarily, of discovering whatever signs there might be of a general improvement, in respect espe- cially of the qualities of consistency, reality, and truth, in other branches of art and manufacture. And without here attempting a recapitulation of what we have attempted at length in the various papers which have been devoted to the subject, we may safely say that upon the whole there is much ground for satisfaction in looking back upon the Exhibition of 1851. While there was much that was debased and impure in style, and faulty as to real principles of design or construction, there was on the other hand ample proof that better and higher principles are beginning to make them- selves apparent; that men are no longer satisfied . with spiritless imitation of precedents, or with ex- ploded formula of taste; but are examining, in all countries and in all departments of industry, more or less, the fundamental laws of fitness, beauty, and truthfulness. And if this be so, there is every reason for hope as to the future. It is not a ques- tion, or at least not yet a question, between this type or style of art and that-between cinque L cento or classical, between Renaissance or Gothic. As yet, the contest is between the I real and the unreal, the truth and the falsehood of art. And in proportion as the better principles . prevail, in whatever form or style the artist frames his work, in that degree the purification of art is advanced; atd whether or no we are ever destined . to see again the universal prevalence of an uniform I style, it will be no little gain if the base, and un- . real, and unfit be discarded by common consent from . the chief branches of human industry. It must be I our hope that the seeds of some such true Renais- , sauce have been widely sown. It has been clearly I manifested that the %workings of such a new prin- I ciple have already shown themselves; and the I Great Exhibitiou has been well timed to develop r its energy. The countries of modern civilization , have compared their several departures from, or their 3 recoveries of, a more true ideal, in the presence of the untutored truthfulnessof semi-barbaric Turkey or Tan is, and the unchanged arts of those older civiliza- . tions of India or China, which, as they have known no i development, so have they experienced no decline or L decay. For our own part, we hope, and we believe, that the result of this competition will be good. ; We wish to express our own conviction that the i revival of truthfulness-of what, in respect of arohi- I tecture, Goethe called Ernsthaftigkeit, or earnest- ness-in art is more conscious and more advanced in our own country than among our neighbours; i while the continental artists, on the other hand, have often, by a less interrupted tradition, retained . much that we have but revived. ECCLESIASTICAL DEPARTMENT OF THE EXHIIBITION.-No. XV.* CONCLUDING PAPER. Having noticed in former papers, under appro- priate heads, the principal contents of the Exhibi- tion sharing aln ecclesiastical character, we have, in conclusion, put together, almost at random, a few additional remarks on topics which have not fallen into the general divisions of the subject. Among the many gratifying retrospects of the Exhibition, we may reckon the evident growing predilection for the use of various granites and marbles, as materials for architectural construc- tion and decoration. Some very beautiful specimens of madrepore and deep chocolate-coloured marble, sent from Mr. Charnpernowne's quarries at Dart- ington, near Totnes, may be especially noticed. But we did not observe any such complete col- lection of the products of our own quarries as was exhibited of all the marbles from the Vosges chain, and again as the interesting spe- cimens of the marbles of the Pyrenees contributed by M. Derville and Co., of Marseilles. From Spain aud Portugal also there were complete col- lections of the marbles of those countries. The marbles of Italy were illustrated in the exquisite mosaics froni Rome and Florence. Among the building materials from our own islands, we noticed the successful application of slate, in unusually thick slabs, to subh purposes as ridge-crests. We were glad to observe a more extensive use of our native marbles in domestic furniture. The Russian specimens of veneering in malachite formed a point of great attraction in the Exhibi- tiou; The piecing together of this very beautiful material is doubtless a not improper treatment of such a substance; but we doubt if it can be cousi- dered in conformity with principles of reality thus to use this ingenious veneering, not merely as a sub- sidiary ornament, but as if mnalachite were itself capable of being cut into huge slabs and used in construction. We should coufine our praise of NM. Demidoff's malachite to the exceeding skill shown in the comlbinatiou of its fragments ; fur not only were soile of its applications most unsuitable, but the style of ornament in which it was worked up, and especially in the concomitant metal work, was of a very corrupt character. It is singular that in the sofa in the Indian Court, formed of Rajpootana marble, this beautiful material was not used in a proper constructional manner, although reality is almost a universal principle in the art of Oriental civilization. The ivory chair, on the contrary, which was placed under the tent in the middle of the Court, was constrncted on a much better principle. Tile horn furniture of Hamburg, whatever may be thought of the propriety or good taste of so using such materials, deserves at least the credit of strict reality of construction. It may be reckoned a step in the right direction that the use of wood, inlaid in patterns, is be- ginning, it would seem, to be revived for purposes of flooring. Modern floors, for the most part, abso- lutely require their ugliness to be concealed by car- pets ; and the custom has been to paint a deal floor oak-colour, if any part is exposed beyond the extent of the carpet on stairs or in dining rooms. Mr. Leistler exhibited an excellent specimen of inlaid flooring in his Austrian suite of rooms: and, as applied also to ecclesiastical or semi-ecclesiastical purposes, the aid of machinery has been very ser- viceably employed by Mr. Pratt, of New Bond- street, iu reducing the price of the " inlaid parquet flooring," of which lie exhibited some specimens. But while on the one hand marbles and other real materials are more freely used than heretofore, on the other bland, we are sorry to say, imitation sub- stances appear to be increasing in number if not in favour. Messrs. Austen and Seeley exhibited a fountain made of their artificial stone, which how- ever (we should think) must have disenchanted any possible admirers of that substance, since under the influence of its spray, it never looked otherwise than damp and green and pervious to water. Equally unsuccessful was a Corinthian capital, in the Enig- lish nave, made of papicr-?naeh6. Its exhibitor, Mr. Bielfield, furnished also numerous specimens of both gothic and classical architectural mouldings and oruaments in the same material. Ill carto m-pierre, M. Mayer, of Munich, exhibited a rather vulgarly designed statue of the Blessed Virgin and Child. Being coloured, the actual ma- terial could never have been guessed. We may mention, also, that the English part of the Exhibition contained all sorts of architectural mouldings, flowers, pendants, &c., made of gutta percha; while another person produced the same in patent stone, or even in leather, under the name of " rolievo leather tapestry." Messrs. Willock and Co., of Manchester, besides the hideous Lever Bridge church, displayed capitals, poppy-heads, &c., in terra cotta. Mr. Denis, of London, imi- tated marble very skilfully in his scagliola. Indeed there appears to be no end of artificial building mia- terials; and the main object of nearly all the ex- hibitors of this kind seems to be to counterfeit in some sham substance the appearance, without the properties, of something else. But with all this, the tide is undoubtedly setting in favour of the principle of reality in construction and ornament. Even railway carriages are now made to depend for decoration on the grain of the wood of which they are constructed, which is brought out and heightened by varnish, instead of being concealed under thick coats of paint. The Great Northern Railway Company was the first, we believe, to iitroduce this at once rational and economical innovation ; but the example has been widely followed by other companies. The Exhibi- tion building contained a beautiful railway carriage by Mr. Williams so finished; and nothing excited more general commendation, we believe, in the carriage department, than a dog-cart which had neither colour nor ornament beyond the fihe grain of the highly-polished and varnished wood of which it was built. Similarly in the department of North Germany, there was a very conspicuous field-piece, mounted on a beau- tifully framed and polished gun-carriage, no paint at all being used, either on the carriage itself, or on the ramrod and other accessories. It should be added, that we were informed by a practical authority that carriages generally would be iore durable if varnished only, and not painted ; and in churches especially it is well known that the dry- rot extends its ravages far more widely and irreme- diably under the deceitful exterior of a coat of paint, than when the woodwork is exposed in its proper substance to the free air. We do indeed hope that we may have seen the beginning of the end of that nearly universal but absurd fashion of " graining"-that is, the clumsy imitation in paint of the grain of oak, and indeed of imitating generally the more expensive and beautiful woods on some cheap and common material. Few people know how really beautiful is the grain even of the common deal- timber, when highly varnished, without, however, any colouring matter being introduced. The design of organ-cases, and the arrangement of their pipes, present a great field for the revival of more true and real principles of construction. The organs in the Exhibition were generally, in this respect, inferior ; but we noticed a chamber- organ, by M. Alexandre, of Paris, in which the pipes were exposed and made part of the design, instead of being concealed behind a sham case. No colour was employed in this example. I have been very much puzzled by one of the decisions. I had remarked, in visiting the Exhibition, an immense floor- cloth, of one entire design, in imitation of an antique tesselated pavement, and formed, in pattern, colour, and arrangement, after the strictest classical model. I said, as I looked at it, "That is what a floor-cloth ought to be. If I had a large hall I would buy it." As a work of decorative art, it was admirable on account of the good taste of its design and its subdued harmony of colour. My opinion I afterwards saw confirmed by a highly eulogistic passage in The Morning Chronicle. As I saw nothing of the same kind equal to it, I of course concluded that in this manufacture, Messrs. Smith and Baber, by whom the specimen was produced, would infallibly obtain the highest medal. They did not; and I should feel very much obliged if some member of the jury who decided on these matters would tell me why? I presume that the judgment of the gentlemen on this occasion must have been fairly given; but for the life of me I cannot conceive any reason why a work of art, which it really was, should have been set aside, and the medal which seemed its due be conferred on a large piece of floor-cloth, consisting of long strips of various patterns, like a tailor's show book, with a picture of one of the Bristol Churches painted as a centre ornament--the most unsuitable thing in the world for such a position, unless, indeed, the article has been prepared for the house of the Dean of Bristol, in which there exists so anxious a desire to tread the Church under foot. ECCLESIASTICAL DEPARTMENT OF THE EXHIIBITION.-No. XV.* CONCLUDING PAPER. Having noticed in former papers, under appro- priate heads, the principal contents of the Exhibi- tion sharing aln ecclesiastical character, we have, in conclusion, put together, almost at random, a few additional remarks on topics which have not fallen into the general divisions of the subject. Among the many gratifying retrospects of the Exhibition, we may reckon the evident growing predilection for the use of various granites and marbles, as materials for architectural construc- tion and decoration. Some very beautiful specimens of madrepore and deep chocolate-coloured marble, sent from Mr. Charnpernowne's quarries at Dart- ington, near Totnes, may be especially noticed. But we did not observe any such complete col- lection of the products of our own quarries as was exhibited of all the marbles from the Vosges chain, and again as the interesting spe- cimens of the marbles of the Pyrenees contributed by M. Derville and Co., of Marseilles. From Spain aud Portugal also there were complete col- lections of the marbles of those countries. The marbles of Italy were illustrated in the exquisite mosaics froni Rome and Florence. Among the building materials from our own islands, we noticed the successful application of slate, in unusually thick slabs, to subh purposes as ridge-crests. We were glad to observe a more extensive use of our native marbles in domestic furniture. The Russian specimens of veneering in malachite formed a point of great attraction in the Exhibi- tiou; The piecing together of this very beautiful material is doubtless a not improper treatment of such a substance; but we doubt if it can be cousi- dered in conformity with principles of reality thus to use this ingenious veneering, not merely as a sub- sidiary ornament, but as if mnalachite were itself capable of being cut into huge slabs and used in construction. We should coufine our praise of NM. Demidoff's malachite to the exceeding skill shown in the comlbinatiou of its fragments ; fur not only were soile of its applications most unsuitable, but the style of ornament in which it was worked up, and especially in the concomitant metal work, was of a very corrupt character. It is singular that in the sofa in the Indian Court, formed of Rajpootana marble, this beautiful material was not used in a proper constructional manner, although reality is almost a universal principle in the art of Oriental civilization. The ivory chair, on the contrary, which was placed under the tent in the middle of the Court, was constrncted on a much better principle. Tile horn furniture of Hamburg, whatever may be thought of the propriety or good taste of so using such materials, deserves at least the credit of strict reality of construction. It may be reckoned a step in the right direction that the use of wood, inlaid in patterns, is be- ginning, it would seem, to be revived for purposes of flooring. Modern floors, for the most part, abso- lutely require their ugliness to be concealed by car- pets ; and the custom has been to paint a deal floor oak-colour, if any part is exposed beyond the extent of the carpet on stairs or in dining rooms. Mr. Leistler exhibited an excellent specimen of inlaid flooring in his Austrian suite of rooms: and, as applied also to ecclesiastical or semi-ecclesiastical purposes, the aid of machinery has been very ser- viceably employed by Mr. Pratt, of New Bond- street, iu reducing the price of the " inlaid parquet flooring," of which lie exhibited some specimens. But while on the one hand marbles and other real materials are more freely used than heretofore, on the other bland, we are sorry to say, imitation sub- stances appear to be increasing in number if not in favour. Messrs. Austen and Seeley exhibited a fountain made of their artificial stone, which how- ever (we should think) must have disenchanted any possible admirers of that substance, since under the influence of its spray, it never looked otherwise than damp and green and pervious to water. Equally unsuccessful was a Corinthian capital, in the Enig- lish nave, made of papicr-?naeh6. Its exhibitor, Mr. Bielfield, furnished also numerous specimens of both gothic and classical architectural mouldings and oruaments in the same material. Ill carto m-pierre, M. Mayer, of Munich, exhibited a rather vulgarly designed statue of the Blessed Virgin and Child. Being coloured, the actual ma- terial could never have been guessed. We may mention, also, that the English part of the Exhibition contained all sorts of architectural mouldings, flowers, pendants, &c., made of gutta percha; while another person produced the same in patent stone, or even in leather, under the name of " rolievo leather tapestry." Messrs. Willock and Co., of Manchester, besides the hideous Lever Bridge church, displayed capitals, poppy-heads, &c., in terra cotta. Mr. Denis, of London, imi- tated marble very skilfully in his scagliola. Indeed there appears to be no end of artificial building mia- terials; and the main object of nearly all the ex- hibitors of this kind seems to be to counterfeit in some sham substance the appearance, without the properties, of something else. But with all this, the tide is undoubtedly setting in favour of the principle of reality in construction and ornament. Even railway carriages are now made to depend for decoration on the grain of the wood of which they are constructed, which is brought out and heightened by varnish, instead of being concealed under thick coats of paint. The Great Northern Railway Company was the first, we believe, to iitroduce this at once rational and economical innovation ; but the example has been widely followed by other companies. The Exhibi- tion building contained a beautiful railway carriage by Mr. Williams so finished; and nothing excited more general commendation, we believe, in the carriage department, than a dog-cart which had neither colour nor ornament beyond the fihe grain of the highly-polished and varnished wood of which it was built. Similarly in the department of North Germany, there was a very conspicuous field-piece, mounted on a beau- tifully framed and polished gun-carriage, no paint at all being used, either on the carriage itself, or on the ramrod and other accessories. It should be added, that we were informed by a practical authority that carriages generally would be iore durable if varnished only, and not painted ; and in churches especially it is well known that the dry- rot extends its ravages far more widely and irreme- diably under the deceitful exterior of a coat of paint, than when the woodwork is exposed in its proper substance to the free air. We do indeed hope that we may have seen the beginning of the end of that nearly universal but absurd fashion of " graining"-that is, the clumsy imitation in paint of the grain of oak, and indeed of imitating generally the more expensive and beautiful woods on some cheap and common material. Few people know how really beautiful is the grain even of the common deal- timber, when highly varnished, without, however, any colouring matter being introduced. The design of organ-cases, and the arrangement of their pipes, present a great field for the revival of more true and real principles of construction. The organs in the Exhibition were generally, in this respect, inferior ; but we noticed a chamber- organ, by M. Alexandre, of Paris, in which the pipes were exposed and made part of the design, instead of being concealed behind a sham case. No colour was employed in this example. We must ex- press both surprise and regret that. Mr. Pugin did not display an organ case in his Medi.Tval Court. The organ erected by him in Jesus College Chapel, Cambridge, is so original in conception and so grace- ful in its colouring that we are sure he could have produced something which would have surpassed his other church furniture, had he but included an organ in his (so-called) medimeval display. I have been very much puzzled by one of the decisions. I had remarked, in visiting the Exhibition, an immense floor- cloth, of one entire design, in imitation of an antique tesselated pavement, and formed, in pattern, colour, and arrangement, after the strictest classical model. My opinion I afterwards saw confirmed by a highly eulogistic passage in The Morning Chronicle. As I saw nothing of the same kind equal to it, I of course concluded that in this manufacture, Messrs. They did not; and I should feel very much obliged if some member of the jury who decided on these matters would tell me why? I presume that the judgment of the gentlemen on this occasion must have been fairly given; but for the life of me I cannot conceive any reason why a work of art, which it really was, should have been set aside, and the medal which seemed its due be conferred on a large piece of floor-cloth, consisting of long strips of various patterns, like a tailor's show book, with a picture of one of the Bristol Churches painted as a centre ornament--the most unsuitable thing in the world for such a position, unless, indeed, the article has been prepared for the house of the Dean of Bristol, in which there exists so anxious a desire to tread the Church under foot. A L young and graceful youth, active as a fawn and vigorous as a gladiator, holds in one arm a pan- ther's cub, whilst the mother, enraged at the ab- straction of her offspring, dashes savagely upon her foe ; 'with a determination, soaring above the pain inflicted by the talons of the animal, the hunter raises his arm to strike a death-blow to his ferocious assailant. Like Gibson's *" Hunter," this group forcibly illustrates the felicity with which the true artist may select the appropriate moment, when intensity of rapid action is implied, rather than absolutely represented. It is always painful to notice iistances in which skill and labour of no ordinary quality are bestowed on works, the original designs of which are unworthy of so lavish an expenditure of either. The head is sufficiently beautiful, but seems rather awkwardly placed upon the shoulders. In thus bringing to a close our hasty enumeration of the leading works of sculpture contributed to the Great Exhibition of all natiODS, we cannot but feel that in art, as in social economy and political de- velopment, we are indeed living in an age of tran- sition. Every student of the fine arts who has visited the great continental galleries possesses the means of judging for himself, and of comparing the characteristics, not only of the existing European schools, but of those which flourished in former ages. With this facility he has no escape from a servile imitation and reproduction of the past, ex- cept by exercising that power of selection with which his reason has endowed him, and by extract- ing originality from new combinations, rather than from attempts to realise eccentric novelty. That species of eclecticism in which the deepest study is combined with the most manly indepen- dence of judgment, is tie form of art-theory adopted by those who have of late years achieved the most imperishable fame. Let us hope that in England we may hereafter prove to the world that we have duly regarded the lessons in art offered for our instruction by our foreign contemporaries, whilst we have not lost sight of those qualities which are strictly national, nor abandoned our- selves to the belief that every variation must needs be an improvement. Passints from these, we next come to the skin of that well-known and useful domestic animal, the cat. The cat, when properly attended to, and bred purposely for its skin, gives a most useful and durable fur. In Holland it is bred and kept in a confined state till the fur attains its greatest perfec- tion, and it is fed entirely onl fish. In other coun- tries, and especially our own, it is produced in large numbers. The wild cat is much larger, and longer in the fur, and it is met with in extensive forests, particularly in Hungary; the colour is grey, spotted with black, and its softness and dura- bility render it suitable for cloak and coat linings, for which purpose it is much used. The value of this skin, and its extensive consumption, have, no doubt, been the cause of the disappearance of many a sleek and fa- vourite "Tabby," and we would recommend those of our readers who are in possession of a pet of this description to keep careful watch and ward over it. Having, in our former notice of this subject, glanced at raw, thrown, and spun silk, together with that manufactured into furniture damasks and brocatelles, we now take the general display of the Spitalfields (or rather metropolitan) silk trade, and shall endeavour to call attention to its more important features as regards both design and execution. Before commencing our detailed notice, however, it will be desirable to say a few words as to the question of design, as applied to silk manufac- tures. That, until very recently, we have been alto- gether dependent upon France for the production of the best designs wrought out by British looms, is as certain as the fact that the French looms, though invented by Jacquard, have been very greatly in- proved by British skill and ingenuity. In fact, beyond the great first principle of its construction-which remains intact because its discoverer left it perfect- the Jacquard machine is a very different one in its practical application from what it was on its intro- duction into this country; and had we but paid a tithe of the attention to the amount of beauty to be produced by the loom, that we have given to the mode of production, design, as applied to silk fabrics, would have been in a very dif- fereut position from that in which we see it at the present time. Content, however, to rely upon others in this matter rather than upon themselves, our manufacturers were, and in a great measure still are, almost slavishly dependent upon the talent of their French neighbours for the very thing they most needed-the means of duly de- l corating the fabrics they manufactured. As we showed in our last notice of this department, so long as this copying system was concealed and covered up by the cloak of Protection, those who practised it cared very little for anything beyond getting hold of the pattern to be copied at the earliest possible moment; and frequently two or three editions of n pirated design have inade their appearance simultaneously-each practitioner considering, until undeceived, that he had stolen a march upon his neighbour. It is not, therefore, l to be wondered at that, with the facilities which Protection or prohibitory tariffs gave for this system, those who adopted it were not precisely I the people to judge or act for themselves in matters of taste; hence, when compelled to design for themselves, they needed some enlightenment as to the most fit and effective results to be arrived aMt, and made many mistakes in learning that which more energy, public spirit, and self-respect ought to have taught them a century ago. Now, however, I we are beginning to see this done, owing to the wise determination to throw an important branch of industry upon its own resources ; and the Exhi- bition affords creditable evidence that we have at least made a commencement, and thought it worth while to attempt to think for ourselves. i There is no better proof of this than the magni-j ficent example of brocade weaving exhibited by I Messrs. Lewis and Allenby, of Regent-street, and manufactured for thein by Messrs. Campbell, Har- rison, and Lloyd. The breadth is a noticeable feature, though this peculiarity is imperfectly seen, owing to the narrow space in which it is exhibited. Effective and artistic in design, clear and brilliant in result, the colouring tastefully arranged, and thrown in with much skill and judgment-this example is noticeable, since it is probably one of the first attempts ever made in this country to cultivate a high style of design and weaving, as applicable to such a fabric as a lady's dress. We shall now endeavour to give a general review l of the ribbons displayed by the representatives of that branch of the British silk trade. These are all contributed from the city of Coventry, and are grouped or arranged together in a uniform case, divided into compartments according to the necessi- ties of each manufacturer. The Coventry people l appear to have taken up the idea of the Exhibition with great spirit; and, in order to show what could be done by the manufacturers and weavers of that place, a subscription was entered into for the l purpose of paying the cost of producing a high class ribbon, which should show that, where price did not put a limit to execution, much more could be done than Coventry had ever had the credit for being able to do. A committee of I manufacturers was appointed to attend to the execution of this specimen, and to arrange for its exhibition. It forms, appropriately enough, the central object in the glass case in which the whole of the contributions, as before stated, are arranged; and it presents some highly creditable features, the weaving being unexceptionable. All modern ribbons, however, appear to us to be based upon a wrong principle in the matter of decoration, and these excessively la- boured attempts at the imitation of flowers are a sign of an utter want of invention and true artistic talent. Geometric arrangements of form, carrying colour as the primary object, would be most applicable to the general uses of a J ribbon, as the purpose is usually that of a border or addition in the way of trimming to some other orna- mental feature of dress. This ribbon, thus manufac- E tured as an example of skill, being in its design of the usual character of such articles, is in reality a dis- tiuct subject in itself, anrd no consideration is given to the fact that it ought to be only a supplemental ornament. In saying this we desire only to call attention to the principle, for it must be readily acknowledged that, as all example of the prevailing style, it is at once rich and effective-no less credit- able to the producers as an example of style, than the motive that prompted its execution was credit- able to their judgment and public spirit. We find that this ultra-imitative tendency prevails throughout nearly all the high-class ribbons. I Messrs. R. S. Cox and Co. make an excellent dis-I play as a whole, but so determined are they that the closeness of the imitation shall be appreciated, that they have placed the originals, extracted from a botanical work, by the side of the woven specimen. A garniture ribbon exhibited by Messrs. Howell aiid James is an excellent example of its class, effective and well arranged. Messrs. Marshall and Snelgrove also exhibit a very admirable ribbon, the pattern upon which is based on the lilac. There is a spottiness about the examples exhibited which is chiefly the result of the contrast in colour being too distinct, and this destroys that delicacy which ought to be a leading feature in a tasteful ribbon. Messrs. Sharp, Odell, and Jury, show examples which1 illustrate this prin- ciple, since their display is injured materially by this violence in contrast. Mr. Charles Bray and Mr. R. Caldicott each make a display of ribbons of the class usually manufactured at Coventry for the ordinary market. These are of good character, and, in many instances, superior to the more ambitious attempts; and the same may be said of the series of ribbons exhibited by Messrs. J. and C. Ratliff, in illustration of the Coventry trade in its most extensive departments. Messrs. Sturdy and Turner show some very bold and effective garniture ribbons, the weaving of which is admi- r able. There is a fatal defect, however, in the drawing of the roses with which one of them is de- corated. Mr. Thomas Robinson and Mr. James Hart also exhibit specimens of a highly praise- worthy character. The gimps, trimmings, and borderings displayed ; by W. and 11. Browett, are tasteful alike in execu- tion and design and in the arrangement of the , whole. |This display, then, of Coveutry mauufacture is 3oie of considerable merit. That more art and a better principle of design are wanting in most-per- haps in all of them-is certain ; but it must be reme-bered that, in a trade of this kind, an im- m11011se nuuler of persons have to be met in the matter of choice-taste we cannot call it; there- fore the manufacturer has to take care to act accordingly, or he would lose his market. Under . these circumstances, incongruity and some little extravagance are pardonable; and though there is much to find fault with in this collection, there is much more to commend. I Reviewing the whole display of silk, as illus- t trated by British manufacturers, there is very r much to congratulate ourselves upon ; and no one f can doubt that this exposition of the state of the silk trade in this country Will bear its fruits in due season, by giving a wholesome stimulus to this a branch of national industry. The experiments connected with the testing of the beam of hollow bricks, put up by Messrs. Bazley White and Co. at the west end of the building, were yesterday resumed in the presence of Major-General Pasley, Mr. fopkins (one of the jurors), Professor Ansted, Mr. Belsbaw, and a number of other scientific gentlemen. The beam, which rests upon two 18-inchi solid brick piers, had a bearing of 21 feet 4 inches l between the piers; it was 2 feet 3 inches at the bottom of the I beam, 1 foot 6 inches at the top, and 4 feet 2 inches in height ; the sectional area of the beam being of exactly the same proportions as the common brick beam, set with Roman cement, at Nine Elms, and which, after stand- ing eighteen months, was broken with a load of 50,652 lbs. The hollow bricks forming the present beam were 4 inches by 1 64 by 9 inches on the outside, the clay being sine-tenths of au inch in thickness ; they were joined together by Portland cement, gauged in equal parts of cement and sand; and fourteen strips of 1J inch hoop iron of a sixteenth of an inch thick ran through the beam between the courses. The ] weight of3 stone slab placed at the top of thebeam, together I with the scale which rested upon it, was 2,460 lbs. The scale was loaded with pigs of hundred and half hundred veight iron. When the load had reached to 41,600 lbs., which it did at a quarter past two o'clock, it then began to crack, and at a quarter past three, when aload of 62,800 lbs. wasapplied,i it broke in the centre. The fracture first commenced in the lower course iu the cement, and proceeded gradually to increase in almost a straight line to the top of the beam, alternately peesing through brick and cement. Of the fourteen bars of iron which ran through the beam, seven were broken and seven were drawn. The stone slab, four inches in thickness, at the top, was broken through the centre, and one of the piers was forced a foot, and the other one inch and a half, out of the perpendicular, by the failing of the beam. The depth of fall of the beam, at the centre where broken, was eight ioches, when it rested upon the l weights with which it was loaded, the two ends remaining perfectly intact. The experiment was considered highly satisfactory by all parties present. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The destruction of this glorious fabric, as to its materials and fittings, is going rapidly on, and it now saddens the heart to look upon it. Many of the Exhibitors and their servants seem to have formed a kind of friendship for each other, and to feel as if there is something sad in parting. All is bustle and hubbub with packinc; and loading carts and vans to bear away the precious products. The great dissatisfaction which was created by the matter of the prizes begins to subside, and the Commissioners have acquired for themselves a lesson for which all Commissioners in future, both in this and in other countries, may profit. It is now clear, that it would have been incomparably better to have had no prizes whatever, leaving it to the public each to act as a judge on his own behalf, and by orders, or otherwise, to have marked his special approval or admiration of the several productions of the genius of the world. The Commissioners, however, on the whole, have done well. Their task was difficult, and the manner in which they have discharged their duties entitles them to great praise. We are not, - lindeed, quite sure whether they have had the acknowledgment which was due to them. The PRINCE and Mr. PAXTON have monopolised all the praise; but much is due to their co-operators. The Commissioners have deemed it but a fair tribute to the exertions of Englishmen who have managed and superintended the particular department of the British Side of the Exhibition, to offer a pecuniary gratuity as an approving acknowledgment of service rendered ; and it was wisely thought to be ungracious not to manifest the same generosity to those who were similarly occupied on the Foreign Side. They have, therefore, issued a Circular to the Foreign Acting Commissioners, containing a similar offer. It would seem, that as far as the replies have come in, the writers have declined for themselves the acceptance of any such gratuity, but state, that they would receive it on behalf of those who acted under them in the management of their portions of the Exhibition. This is right ; forasmuch as subordinates, more especially family men, have been subjected to not a little inconvenience, and, we presume, to a considerable increase of expense, by so lengthened a sojourn in the Crystal Palace, for the amusement and instruction of the general Public.
