(OFFICIAL INQUIRY. ) Yesterday morning Mr. Otway, the active superintendent of the C division of police, made an official inquiry at the residence of Col. North, No. 16, Arlington-street, Piccadilly, for the purpose of ascertaining the amount of damage done by the unfortunate balloon accident on Monday evening. epon going over the mansion Mr. Otway found, in the front of the house which faces the Green-park, that between fourteen and fifteen feet of the parapet had been torn away, the stones from which had been thrown upon the roof, which they carried in, together with the rafters supporting it, the whole of which were hurled down the staircase into the hall below. Two large stacks of chimneys were also thrown down, the materials of which they were composed falling on the glass roof of the fore-court, which it damaged to a very considerable extent; the roof of the house is damaged in several places by the falling of bricks from the chimneys. Col. North estimates that the damage done to his house alone will amount to upwards of 3001. The damage done to the houses in Park-place, which abuts on Arlington-street, consists chiefly of broken roofs, occasioned by the chimney-pots and iron cowls falling on them. Mr. Otway states that it is impossible to estimate the precise amount of damages done, as there are so many little fractures to the buildings in addition to the more extensive injuries. Colonel North's builder had an interview with Mr. Batty yesterday respecting the cost of the repairs of the Gallant Colonel's house, but the result of the negotiations did not transpire. Although Mrs, Graham is not allowed to hold conversation with any one, yet she kindly wrote the following letter, and placed it in the hands of our reporter:— " TO THE: EDITOK OF THE MORNING , I'OST. " I beg to forward you as correct an account as possible respecting the ascent of the balloon from the Hippodrome, yesterday. It is well known that the wind blew almost a hurricane at times during the day, so much so, that whilst the inflation was proceeding, upwards of thirty men, who were holding ois, were constantly . blown to various parts of the circle by the power of the wind on the balloon. At such times it is totally impossible to ascertain the buoyant power at the time of starting by the usual method of weighing. When we arose, the wind carried us against a high mast or pole in the ground, before we had time to cast our ballast, and a long rent was caused in the upper part of the balloon. We cast out sand to clear the trees in Kensington Gardens, and finding ourselves approaching the Crystal Palace, we gradually discharged the ballast with our hands, so that no great weight should fall in any one spot. We succeeded in quite clearing it, and then made for a descent in the Park, which we effected on the grass, and threw out the long line of our safety bag (without anything being attached) to some men who were running. Two of them caught this line and held on for a short time, but being dragged along by the force of the wind they let go, and we directly rebounded, the wind carrying us on to a house in Arlingtonstreet, and from thence to one in Park-place, where the car rested between a stack of chimneys and a V roof, where we remained until some policemen of the C and some gentlemen's servants came to our assistance, and aided us with ladders to descend through a trap-door, when two eminent medical gentlemen of the neighbourhood promptly attended and rendered us the most kindly aid professionally at such a trying moment. Allow me to add, that the grapnel iron we never let from the car, as can be proved by those who assisted us on the roof, it never having been untied from the side of the car, as we were too anxious to prevent any accident occurring to the men who were running after us. Neither did we touch any part of the Crystal Palace. With regard to any accidents that have occurred to myself in my numerous ascents, I have only confidently to declare that I have met with no more than the most experienced aeronaut of the day, all being liable to mischances, particularly upon such a boisterous day as yesterday. In conclusion, allow me to add that I had arranged with a young lady of family to ascend with me yesterday, who arrived in her carriage a little before six for the purpose, when I declined allowing her to ascend, solely on account of the state of the weather • and told her that on such an evening I would not takei a stranger for 1001., or any other sum that might be offered. A gentleman connected with the Opera-house was with this lady, and gave me credit for my conscientious declaration.—l am, yours, obediently, " M. GRAHAM. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Autograph letters of a highly complimentary character have, we understand, been addreEsed by his Royal Highness Prince Albert to Colonel Reid, Mr. Cole, Mr. Dilke, Dr. Lyon Playfair, Mr. Digby Wyatt, and Colonel Lloyd. In these the Prince, we understand, uses the most gratifying expressions of acknowledgment for the services which the gentlemen named have rendered in carrying to a successful close the work of the Exhibition. His Royal Highness announces his intention of presenting each with a gold medal in commemoration of his connection with them; and to Dr. Lyon Playfair he offers the position of Gentleman Usher, vacant in his household by the appointment of Colonel Reid to the Governorship of Malta. The work of removal proceeds in the Crystal Palace with a rapidity which would hardly be credited except by one who attended from day to day to witness the progress made. The Knightsbridge road is now as much blocked up with vans and waggons as it was some days since with cabs and omnibuses, and the strarge variety of their lading gives ample food for the curiosity of the passers by. Now a costly mirror, then an elaborate specimen of oak carving, and immediately after a curious piece of machinery may be seen moving along in slow procession, while the pathways are covered with porters bearing away the more portable articles. The omnibus men console themselves for the decay of trade by making characteristic jokes about the dead lion. One of them, yesterday, in answer to the question of a passenger as to where all the goods were going, said, "It was only the Exhibition had got the broker in." Within, a long hoarding runs down each side of the nave, and behind it numbers of men may be seen busy at work, nailing down cases and securing packages. The British section is almost a desert, so rapid has been the clearing out. An idea of the dispatch used may be gathered from the fact that from this department alone the goods of 1025 exhibitors were cleared out yesterday. As may be imagined the goods were of the most miscellaneous description. We were much struck with one small glass case, which along with many other curious things had escaped previous inspection. It contained the stuffed 'skin of " Tiney," certainly the smallest full-grown dog in the- world, the property of Sir Archibald INPLaine, who had sent if in rather late for exhibition. It is not three inches long, and might have served as a lapdog for the Queen of Lilliput. In the foreign nave, symptoms of movement also become perceptible. All the imperial contributions in the Russian section are packed, the custodians being anxious to anticipate the rigour of a northern winter. The statues in the nave have all become veiled figures, being securely muffled up in calico, and foreign commissioners may be seen in every direction superintending the work of removal. The police have made an arrangement by which the English exhibitors are shut out from the foreign side, and the foreigners from the British, the object being to prevent any confusion during the removal of goods. In the French department the exhibitors are keeping shop and selling their goods with considerable rapidity. All traces of the crystal fountain, as well as of its successor, the platform, have disappeared from the transept; and it did not escape notice, that the flooring has been most carefully relaid, rather a curious circumstance if the palace be doomed to speedy demolition. It is also mentioned that a large sewer is to be built to carry off the sewerage. Rumours of banquets and balls fly about, rumours of everything, in fact, but the destruction of the edifice. Something cheerful will certainly be expedient to disperse the storm that is rapidly gathering round the heads of the devoted jurors. It is generally asserted that these bodies acted without any common principle to guide them; that in their distress they appealed to the committee of chairmen, who gave them a rule, only to be immediately rescinded by the Royal commissioners. Six out of the 10 members forming the musical jury have forwarded a protest to the Royal Commission, in consequence of their award of the great medal to the house of Broadwood, for its improvements in pianofortes and pianoforte making, having been annulled by the Council of Chairmen. The jurors by whom this protest has been signed are Sir Henry R. Bishop, Dr. Schafhaeutl, Commissioner from Bavaria and Juror, Chevalier Sigismond Neukomm, W. S. Bennett, Cipriani Potter, and Sir G. T. Smart. Chevalier Claussen is also in the field. The watchmakers have declared open war, and there are also strong symptoms of disaffection in the Potteries. Mr. Baxter, the inventor of the beautiful method of printing in oil colours, complains, and as is generally thought with justice, that he has not received a medal in his section. His beautiful collection of specimens will be remembered by all who have visited the fine arts courts, and have received the approving fiat of the illustrious president of the commission. Mr. Baxter has presented his exhibit to the commissioners and they have been graciously pleased to accept it, although they have not deemed it worthy of a medal. The public have shown more discrimination, by purchasing about 30,000 of his Exhibition prints. Mr. Copeland wonders how his matchless statuettes in Parian escaped the piercing eyes of the jurors, when distributing council medals, and several other exhibitors complain that their stands were not even visited previous to the awards. Even the arrangement of the medals themselves is found fault with. It is alleged that at first there were to have been first, second, and third class medals, and that satsequently, when the third class was abolished, all the interior articles in that class were stuffed into the second, and got equal honours with the productions in that class. But these are only the first symptoms of the approaching tornado. It is said that the hapless jurors are about to publish their reasons, a course winch will inevitably make "confusion worse confounded." They should remember Lord Mansfield'a dictum. "Give your opinion, but never give your reasons." It could hardly have been expected that when prizes were being distribute& the non-recipients would be easily satisfied; but in the present case there is a very general current of public opinion in disinterested quarters against many of the awards.

_." THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Both Colonel Reid end Mr. Dilke have, we understand, declined the remuneration for their valuable services offered them by the Royal Commission. The former does so on the ground that, be'ng retained in the Government pay while acting as Chairman of the Executive Committee, he was bound in a measure by military etiquette to act on behalf of the Exhibition without any additional emolument. The latter, with singular disinterestedness, has given his time talents to the great undertaking gratuitously, as a matter of personal feeling, preferring to do so, and being fortunately able to afford that sacrifice. Mr. Cole accepts the o ff er o f the Royal Comm i ss i on, an d d oes so in a spirit with which the public, we are sure, will readily sympathise. His Government salary has been suspended (luring his labours in the service of the Royal Commission, and his private means do not enable him to decline terms of remuneration which no one can doubt that he has far more than earned. Mr. Cole has, from the outset, been the master-spirit or the Exhibition, being, more than any other single indi• vidual, its originator, and impressing upon it more largely and decisively than any one else the character and shape which it has mourned. Colonel Reid has had the order of K.C.B. conferred Upon him, and the Government, making atonement for former injustice, and recognising at the same time his services at the Crystal Palace, have appointed him to the Governorship of Malta. He leaves, therefore, his present duties in a few days, and proceeds to his command in the Mediterranean. Mr. Cole has a moderate pecuniary remuneration from the Commission, and the Companionship of the Bath from His Sovereign, as the reward of his labonrs. Mr. Duke remains unrecom• pensed. Impressed with a conviction that civil services do not receive that consideration from the Crown, as the fountain of honour, to which they are manifestly entitled, he adopts a course which at least leaves him the satisfaction of reflecting, that he has worked most disinterestedly and most ably in a public position of great responsibility. The course which he has adopted will be questioned by some and approved by others; but it must tend to fix more attention upon the subject of honorary distinctions than has hitherto been paid to them in this country. Mere knighthood cannot be regarded as a high object of ambition to sterling merit, and, from the Order of the Bath, public benefactors, if not also State servants, are excluded.— Times. We beg to draw attention to the following letter, and to the signatures attached to it: — To THE EXECTITIVE COMMITTEE OF THE EXHIBITION OF THE INDUSTRY Or ALL NATIONS. London, Oct. 16. Gea tlemen,—Understanding that Her Majesty's Commissioners propose forming a collection of the raw produce of different countries shown in the Great Exhibition, we beg leave to express our conviction of the high practical value of this plan. We anticipate great benefits to merchants, manufacturers, and brokers from the formation of a great trade museum or collection, of which this would be the foundation, and in which specimens of the natural productions or exports of all countries should be deposited, together with Such accurate scientific, practical, and commercial information as can be procured. Such a museum would at all times give the most valuable aid to the mercantile community, and afford that information which is so constantly required, and which there is now no means of obtaining. We would beg to suggest, that, in order to render such a Collection really available for trade purposes, it should be formed in the City of London, and so situated as to be conveniently accessible to those who want to refer to it. The coroner's inquest was resumed on Friday at the Municipal Hall, Chesterfield, John Thompson, guard of the passenger train, deposed:— "We left Derby at twenty minutes past nine. The proper time was five minutes. Ido not , know where the fifteen minutes had been lost. When we got opposite the Clay. Cross station I noticed the slackening of the engine. When we had gone 150 or 200 yards the train stopped. I put my head out and went to the engine driver, lord asked " what's the matter?" He did not know exactly the cause. He examined the wheels and pump, and then said there, was something amiss with the rod. I asked him how long it would ho before he was ready to go on. The fireman said ho thought it would be 10 minutes, and the driver said "a few minutes." I asked him if I should have occasion to go back with the signal, , and the driver said "Yes, you had better." I got into the van to get my lamp and got 30 or 40 yards beyond our train, when the driver or the fireman shouted from the engine "all right." In return I shouted "Is all right P" and commenced going back. When I had got a short distance back I hoard the approach of a train. I had not seen or heard the tram before I turned back. Our train was moving on then. I continued waving my red signal till I got on the foot-board of the last carriage. I then shouted to the driver, "Make speedmake all the haste you can, there is a train coming.' We were moving; and had got a short distance when the other train ran into us. It was coming, faster than I thought. The driver of that, train could see our red tail lamp as well us my: hand-signal lamp. There was a tail-lamp, and two side signal lamps to our train. I had turned back .before heard the goods-train corning. I walked back with my red signal-lamp turned towards the Clay-Cross Tunnel. The train consisted of four carriages and a van." Under crossexaMination, the Witness said : 7 -" When we came to a stand it was about 150 yards this side Clay-Cross Station. We were a quarter of an hour late at starting from Derby, and we had lost ten minutes on the road. When I set off back to walk half a ,mile, I got into my van, and took two fog signals with me.—Ought you not to have taken four ? We. do sometimes. , I have a copy of the rules given tome. I have seen the rule that we are to place a fog signal on the line every 200 yards, till we have got 800 yards. I only took two because I knew I had not to go beyond the tunnel. I got within 100 yards of the platform berm) I turned back. I think Isould run 200 yards in fivu minutes. 1 had only one minute togo out before I turned back. I had consuined three of the four or five minutes that we were stopping by waiting to see what was amiss with the engine: I think the goods train had come up to MI in half the time they should have done, or less than that. I have not told any one that the reason of my turning back was that I hoard a whistle blow. I think I have always given the same account about the affair as now. We are generally late; but the delay is gene ra lly i n l eav i ng Derby.' , Samuel Stratton, who drove the luggage train, deposed:— "The train consisted of 10 trucks and a guard's break. It was a light train. My regular time for leaving Derby is 10 minutes past 0. I saw a passenger train go off. We stood waiting at Derby for it. We followed . it slowly about half a mile to the junction, where We stopped 5 minutes. The next place we stopped at was Belper. We stopped about 5 minutes. Our guard there told us to go on steady to Ambergate. At Ambe.rgate the Oder stood on the platform and told us to look out at Wingfield, as the passenger train was going to stop there. I shut off the steam about half-way through the Clay. cross tunnel, and ran steadily through. At the north side of the tunnel all appeared right, . The two white lights were on at the north end of the tunnel, signifying all right. I then put on the steam. When I got' under the bridge on this side of Clay-Cross station," saw four red lights—the tail light and two side lights of the:passenger train, and the hand lamp of the guard. I saw them all at the same moment, and immediately reversed the engine, and put on the steam, and did all I could to stop. I also called to my fireman. That was just as we got under the bridge. Notwithstanding all that we ran into the other train, saw we could not stop in time. I believe they were in motio n a t th e ti me . Our en-, gine was thrown oil' the line." in his cross•examination, he said:— "I have boon a luggage-train driver only a fortnight. I had boon a fireman years. I had driven to Lincoln a week before, and was practising in the yard "shunting" a week before that. I did not stop at Ambergate, but went steadily past. I ought to have been at Clay-cross at 31 minutes past ten. I believe it was half-past when I got there. I looked at my watch as soon as I got off my engine. I found it was 30 minutes past ten. That was two or three minutes after the collision. We are allowed to run between 20 and 30 miles an hour from Derby to Chesterfield. When I first saw the red lights I was between 150 and 200 yards off the passenger train. I was running at 18 or 20 Miles an hour. I had just put on my steam on seeing the white light at the station. The guard regulates our time on the road. We stop at no station between Derby and Chesterfield. We stopped at Belper because the red light was on. I was about 150 or 200 yards off when I first saw the signals. it would take me about a quarter of a mile to pull up. If the guard had turned on the semaphore light at the station I believe we could have stopped in tune." THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The number of persons who entered the building yesterday was 57,849, and the receipts at the doors amounted to 2,8001. 16s. A serious question has arisen as to the period at which the Exhibition should close. On the one hand, exhibitors from Russia and the northern States of Germany are anxious to have the power of removing their goods after the end of September, as if the Crystal Palace remains open till the middle or end of October, the winter frosts will have set in before they can possibly have them conveyed back to their respective countries; on the other hand, the French are desirous to have the final closing delayed as long as is practicable. They have been late in getting their department thoroughly arranged, and it is a matter of much importance to them that the public should have the fullest opportunity of examining its details. It was understood that the Commission had a short time ago fixed upon the 14th or 15th of ()etcher as the proper period for closing, nor does it seem on the whole desirable that that event should take place at an earlier date, but some arrangement might be come to by which difficulties might be avoided. For instance, those States that were anxious to remove their contributions might have the facilities for so doing afforded to them after the 30th of September, and means might bo adopted for that purpose without closing the doors of the Crystal Palace against the public. It is an obvious and undeniable hardship upon many of the German and Russian contributors that they should have their goods detained until all means for their removal aro cut off by the winter ice, and every disposition we are sure exists on the part of the Commission to meet their wishes and interests. But this question raises others of great importance, the settlement of which cannot be long delayed. The vast expense which the Exhibition has entailed upon exhibitors renders them naturally anxious to have the means of disposing of their contributions in the building when the objects for which they have been displayed are completely satisfied. Whether such sales can properly take place under the circumstances is a matter which the Commission must speedily determine. As far as that body itself is concerned, such an accommodation would be found very convenient in helping to clear out the interior, but it seems doubtful whether the hopkeepers of London would much relish the idea of flinging suddenly into the market so large and valuable a quantity 'of foreign goods. The Marquis of Anglesey will hear with a feeling of satisfaction that if our cousins beat us in yacht-building, they are equally pre-eminent in the manufacture of artificial legs. In the latter branch of industry their Superiority will not be grudged, and they really owe society some act of reparation for having introduced among us Colt's revolvers. The artificial leg patented by Mr. Palmer is, in its way, a most admirable, ingenious, and philanthropic contrivance, and its invention is so remarkably characteristic of the country from whence it comes, that we cannot resist the temptation of inviting attention to it. The patentee in some way or other lost his leg, and, having tried the best substitutes hitherto devised for such a case, like a true American, he set himself to think whether he could not improve upon them. His study of the subject was crowned with the most striking success, and he exemplifies that success in his own person by walking about almost without any perceptible lameness, and with an apparent ease and comfort which are truly surprising. He publishes annually at Philadelphia a journal, which he calls Palmer s Patent Artificial Leg Reporter and Surgical Adjuvant. This curiously entitled periodical accompanied a specimen of the leg to the Exhibition, and the Ist chapter of vol. 3, No. 1, we find commenced by this heading, "Fugitive thoughts on amputation." From another chapter, entitled " Synopsis of the invention," we gather that it is distinguished by its perfect combination of lightness with strength, and by the extraordinary fidelity with which it imitates nature. Having closely examined it we can testify to its merits on all the leading points specified, nor have we any reason to doubt that the enamelled surface of this leg, as stated, " is rivalled only by the mechanism of nature, and that a lady may wear silk hose and slippers without betraying the loss she has sustained." Mr. Palmer has received extensive orders for his patent in this country, and the public may soon expect to see timber-toed veterans no more stumping about Greenwich or Chelsea. The dentist who fills the beauty's mouth with a set of pearly teeth, and the artist who dyes the grey or red head, and covers baldness with an artificial profusion of looks, have now added t o th e i r amiable deceptions those o f American artificial leg, which may occasionally lead to awkward mistakes, but cannot fail to be regarded as a great boon to suffering humanity. The subjoined protest was drawn up, signed, and sent to the Royal Commissioners of the Exhibition, by six out of the ten members forming the musical jury (class X. A.), on learning that their award in favour of Messrs. Broadwood had been annulled by the Council of Chairmen:— "TO HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS THE PRINCE ALBERT, K G &C., &C., &C, PRESIDENT; AND " TO THE ROYAL COMMISSIONERS OF THE GREAT EXHIBITION OF THE WORKS OF INDUSTRY OF ALL NATIONS, 1851. "May it please your Royal Highness, my Lords and Gentlemen, "The jury Class X. A., consisting of the following members —Sir H. It. Bishop (chairman and reporter), Sir George Smart, M. Thalberg, Mr. Cipriani Potter, Mons. Berlicz, le Chevalier ; Neukomm, Dr. Schafhault, Mr. W. Sterndale Bennett, Dr. Black, Dr. Henry Wylde (of whom all were present except Dr. Black and Dr. Wylde)—decided unanimously to award the great medal to the house of Broadwood, for its successful improvements in pianofortes and pianoforte. making. Dr. Black subsequently declared, in the jury. room, his agreement with the award of his colleagues. This decision of the jury was confirmed in the meeting of the group. "The Council of Chairmen, however (as it has been generally reported), rejected the award thus doubly confirmed, and in seeking for the grounds of this rejection the jurors of Class X. A. who transmit these papers, are compelled to state it as their opinion, that undue weight must have been attributed to misstatements made at the meeting of the group, in the presence of many of the chairmen, affecting Messrs. Broadwood's claim as improvers of the pianoforte. The mis-statements were upon remonstrance withdrawn; but it is a lamentable fact, that the injurious effect of such statements positively put forth can seldom be completely effaced by a retractation. "Should such a decision of the Council of Chairmen respecting Messrs. Broadwood be reported to the Royal Commissioners the jurors who transmit this memorial beg most respectfully to be allowed to point out to his Royal Highness and the Royal Commissioners, that in this case a decision, which was arrived at after due deliberation by the jury Class X. A., specially qualified, and seleeted in consequence of technical knowledge of the objects to be submitted to its judgment, and which received subsequent confirmation from the group of associated juries, has been set aside by a body of gentlemen, who, distinguished as they are for their general attainments, may have no special and technical knowledge of pianofortes and pianoforte-making, nor have they in their capacity of chairmen (except the chairman of Class X. A., whose opinion and statements ought to have had due weight) even inspected or been called upon to become acquainted with the instruments upon which the award which they rejected was made. In spite of this fact the responsibility of the award will still probably, in the eyes of the public, rest with the primary jury, and the memorialising jurors, feeling that their professional and scientific reputation would be compromised by a decision so contrary, in their opinion, to the merits of the case, and which will, they are sure, astonish the whole s European musical world, earnestly entreat his Royal Highness and the Royal Commissioners to take the case into their consideration, and to apply to it such remedy as may seem best fitted in their judgment. " With this statement is transmitted an extract from the official document setting forth the special mechanical improvements on which Messrs. Broad wood's claims are founded. And the memorialising jurors conclude by expressing their conviction the house of Messrs. Broad wood has eminently fulfilled every single condition contained in the instructions to the juries, combining in their instruments novelty of invention (of considerable importance and usefulness), perfection of workmanship, beauty of design, and superior quality of tone.' TO THE EDITOR OF THE MORNING HERALD. have seen this morning a letter to an exhibitor, from M. Digby Wyatt, Esq., stating that as the juries of the Great Exhibition have long since been dismissed, there is now no such thing as redress for those exhibitors who may feel disappointed in the non-award of prizes for things exhibited by them at the Great Exhibition. Then sir, let every exhibitor, who styles himself inventor, designer, improver, or maker of anything of regular or artistic form, whether made from one or more materials, at once repudiate the reception of the common Exhibition medal, that same, which might have been by them obtained at infinitely less cost, hazard, time, patience, or skill, by their simply sending a specimen of any one of the thingsthe commonest raw produce. And, sir, if after such repudiation the executive committee or the present constituted authorities, whoever they may be, persist in sending to those exhibitors who may be inventors, designers, improvers, or makers of anything, let them, sir, Ist. Cut such medals in half, and 2dly. Send the one-half to the foreign jurors, and the other to the British. Then possibly, sir, the several juries may re-assemble, and group their several parts into a monument, with an appropriate inscription, dedicated To the Struggles of Genius in Adversity. I am, Mr. Editor, your obedient servant, WILLIAM EDWARD HALL, Class VIII., No. 73. 55, Great Marylebone-street, Oct. 16, 1851.

THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Saturday, owing to the inclemency of the weather, the unusually small sum of 1,3601. 15s. was taken at the doors of the building, the whole number of visitors being 9,326. The aspect which the interior now presents on the last day of the week is a sufficiently striking contrast to the crowds of shilling visitors who flock there between Monday and Thursday. All is comparative quietness and repose, and the greatest bustle caused is by the movement in different directions of invalid chairs, the feeble occupants of which seem to enjoy the magnificent spectacle presented to them almost like a promise of returning health and strength. Mr. Belshaw's elephant has at last arrived from Essex, and been comfortably located in the Indian compartment. He had not been au hour in the building when steps were taken to give him a truly oriental equipment, and before the doors were closed on Saturday evening he was completely covered with costly trappings. Mr. Belshaw will without delay have the Newab Nazim of Bengal's magnificently carved ivory Howdah placed upon his back, and will call in the aid of some experienced Indian in getting him properly caparisoned. From what we hear, our plate-glass manufacturers are likely to be entirely distanced by those from Circy and St. Gobain, in France—a defeat altogether unexpected, but about tho justice of which there seems to be no doubt. The French also show some oxide of zinc glass, the transparent, colourless beauty of which is very remarkable, and which merits the more praise from its novelty. The attention of chemists and others interested in the subject has been much arrested by a new preparation, called amorphous phosphorus, and by which all the difficulty encountered in the transport and use of phosphorus for manufacturing purposes, as in the making of lucifer matches, is removed. This preparation is the discovery of a M. Schrotter, who obtains it by heating phosphorus, in the absence of air, to the temperature of an oil bath. It then becomes of a scarlet colour, and can be carried about or packed into barrels, or even taken into the system, without any injurious effects. Mixed with any oxidizing substance it recovers its burning properties. HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY OF LONDON. THE JULY FETE AT CHISWICK. This, the third and last fete of the Horticultural Society, took place on Saturday, and the visitors were, as usual on such occasions, favoured with about as moist an afternoon as one often meets with in the month of July. Notwithstanding the threatening appearance of the weather, the company poured into the gardens in larger numbers than usual, up to half-past three o'clock, and had not the clouds at length discharged their unwelcome contents, there is little doubt that this would have been one of the most crowded meetings ever held in these gardens. The attendance, as it was, was numerous and highly fashionable; the dresses of th'e ladies were most elegant, but of far too light a texture to enable them with any comfort to enjoy the promenade in the Duke of Devonshire's grounds, which, as usual on the fete day, were thrown open by his Grace for the benefit of the visitors, the atmosphere during the whop afternoon, even prior to the commencement of the rain, being so cold as to induce most of the fair sex to avail themselves of the shelter of the tents in which the plants, &e., were exhibited. There were, as usual, three regimental bands present, viz., the Ist Life Guards, the Royal Horse Guards (blue), and the band of one of the household regiments, and the selections of music, which were in great taste, were admirably performed. The exhibition of plants, flowers, and fruits was fully equal to anything of the kind that has ever come under our notice. The must beautiful among the plants, we think, were the exotic orchids and the heath. Among the fruits, the pines and strawberries attracted the greatest notice, and most deservedly, for among the pines were two grown by Mr. Jones, of Enville, weighing respectively 81b. 9oz. and 101 b., and one by Mr. Briddon, weighing 91b. We were unable to obtain a list of the aristocratic visitors, but we recognised many of the nobility and families of the highest distinction. We also observed an'unusually large muster of foreigners, who appeared to take great interest in the exhibition, and were evidently much delighted with the rare and curious plants, of which there was a very large display. Taking the Jae as a whole, wo think, leaving the drawback of the weather out of the question, the result of the day's proceedings must have been highly satisfactory to the society. The t e nts a n d marquees were, as usual, supplied from the manufactory of Mr. B. Edgington, of the Borough, and proved most efficacious in protecting the company from the heavy showers, &c. The following farewell letter has. been received! by the Executive Comnmittee of the Exhibition off Industry of all Nations, from Mr. Riddle, the United States Comnmissioner, previous to his depar- ture for New York:- "To the Executive Committee of the Great Exhibition. Gentlemen-As my official duties in the Crystal Palace have now ceased, I shall take my departure for America on the 12th inst. I cannot allow myself to go hence without tendering you my sincere and heartfelt acknovwedgments for the many acts of kindness, courtesy, and attention I have received at your hands, and for the uniform promptness with which you have responded to all, communications emanating from this Commission. Indeed, in my humble opinion, the success of the Great Exhibition may be mainly. attributable to the admirable and indefatigable management of your committee, and the limited number of gentlemen of which it was composed, thereby preventing collisions which would inevitably have occurred had the whole responsibility been entrusted to a larger body of directors. While I have received every assistance from officers under your directions, there is one who has been high in authority, and of whom I cannot speak in too high terms of praise. I allude to Cap- tain Owen, of the Royal Entineers. The even temper, and calm, dignified, demeanour he has observed on all trying and pressing occasions, are worthy of the highest commen- dation ; and for one, I am proud to bear witness of the ener. getic and impartial manner in which he has discharged his arduous duties. " Wishing each and all of you, gentlemen, that continued success to which your brilliant talents so justly entitle you, I have the honour to subscribe myself, very respectfully, your obedient servant, (Signed) " EDWARD RIDDLE, United States Commissioner to the Industrial Exhibition. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Yesterday the crowd which thronged every tho- roughfare leading to the Crystal Palace was larger probably than on any day since the 1st of May. From 9 to 11 o'clock, the road from Park-lane to the south entrance was covered with omnibuses and cabs so closely packed as to move in one slow moving mass. TIrhe park was traversed by great numbers of pedestrians, who preferred its cool green to the noisy, hot, dusty road. The appearance of the Crystal Palace itself at once gave promise of a very crowded attendance, which was realised so early, that by eleven o'clock 13,500 persons had entered. As many more passed in during the next hour, so that by 12 o'clock 27,000 visitors had been admitted. The next hour brought 8,500 visitors, and the increase was maintained during the day. Although probably more persons passed in at the doors than on any provious day, the building was by no means so inconveniently crowded; and the commission- ers may yet find that even. more than their hypothetical 60,000 maybe received. Order, and a disposition to give and take, impart a wond-rful elasticity to the accommoda- tion of crowds. At the stilling price, too, the proportion of visitors who love to pursue their observations for a few hours during a larger number of days, rather than protract their stay in the building, is much greater than before; and as some of these prefer the morning, and others the' after part of the day, a continued stream to and fro is main- tained. The galleries rernain the least frequented part of the building, from the natural indisposition of most persons to ascend them before the interest of the objects on the ground floor has been comparatively exhausted. It might become a question for the executive committee, in case of an inconvenient overcrowding, how to compensate this dis- advantage of the upper portion of the building so as to relieve the lower area. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The beautiful autumnal weather of Monday attracted an enormous crowd to the Great Exhibition. The throng of vehicles was immense, and it was observed that the streams of pedestrians were more dense and continuous than on any previous occasion. The inference drawn from this latter circumstance is; that the people of London itself are now beginning to supply the vacuum created by the exhaustion of the provinces. A remarkable instance of the intense curiosity which the Great Exhibition has excited in the minds of even the poorest of the people was afforded in the case of a poor fishwoman, named Mary Cahinack, from the parish of Paul, in Cornwall,:wbo, although in the eighty-fourth year of her age walked the whole distance (350 miles) for the purpose of visiting the Crystal Palace. She was among the crowd on Monday, an d went about with al .avidity that gave little indica- tion of weariness or old age. It appears that on Tuesday she went to the Mansion house, to see the Lord Mayor and obtain some relief to help her on her journey home, all her money being gone except 54.d. The Lord Mayor, after hearing herstory, kindly gave her a sovereign, and she was moreover hospitably entertained in the housekeeper's ?? machinery room on Monday was, as is always the case on shilling days, densely crowded: all the machines were at work, and the people watched their intricate operations with every appearance of attention and enjoyment. The police numbers were 59,344, and the receipts 2,8631 6s.-On Tuesday upwards of 60,000 persons passed the barriers, and comfortably filled every nook and corner of the vast edifice. A peculiarity in the attendance now begins to develop itself, which was not perceptible in the early days of the Exhibition. While the throng of omnibuses and cabs continues as dense as ever, the tide of pedestrians swells daily, so as to render the thoroughfares pearly impassable to any one who attempts to breast the current. There can be no doubt but that the London tradesmen and mechanics now begin to flock thitherwards in right earnest. There were immense numbers of them, with their families, among the visitors on Tuesday, and the number of babies in arms was such as to render all fears for the consequences of the emigration drain quite superfluous. The quota of schools was rather large, and comprised the St Matthew's, Denmark hill, 39 girls; National, Stockwell, 38 boys, 35 girls; Crown street British, 24 boys : larlowv, Essex, 26 girls and boys; IKensall-green National, 32 boys ; St John's (servants), 22 boys: Barnard and Fawbert's, Harlow, Essex, 87 boys and girls; St John's Wood, Roman Catholic, 24 boys; Southampton National, 24 boys. Amongst the general visitors the only group requiring particular notice was the Chinese family from Albert gate, who appeared in full costume, and had quite as many admirers as the Koh-i-noor. Another point of attraction was a large board which the executive committee had caused to be placed at the southern entrance, and upon which was displayed in large conspicuous figures the number of visitors for each day of the week, and for every successive hour of the day. Its utility soon became apparent to the various officials, who were saved the trouble of telling every one who went out the exact figure up to his or her departure. The arrangements for the final closing of the Exhibition become of greater interest as the day fixed for the nurnose apDroaches. We believe that, as they stand at present, the ltlh, which falls on Satulrday, will be no other;ise distinguished than by an absolute prohibition of invalid chairs, and the opening of the doors at nine o'clock, instead of twelve, as at present. The evening's closing will be final as regards the public, and on the following Wednesday Prince Albert will attend to distribute the medals, and to take his leave of the exhibitors and jurors. This, we believe, will comprehend the entire closing ceremonial. The police numbers were 60,382, and the receipts, 2,8591. 7s.-The receipts on Wednesday amounted to 2,5721. 12s., and the number of visitors was 54,540.-The number of visitors to the building on Thursday, was 57,161, and the amount received 2.7251. 14s. The 'Daily News' says that there is a rumour that the Exhibition is to be kept open a supplemental week or fortnight for the benefit of the excluded classes. The old phrase. of scriptural authority, relative to "spoiling the Egyptians," was amus- ingly reversed on Thursday, in the case of a family of Egyptian Arabs, consisting of a tall old sheik in most oriental tatters, two or three women jealously concealed in voluminous linen, by no means of the whitest, and four little boys, who bossted that their faces had siever been washed since their birth, and gave ocular demonstration of the truth of their assertion. On arriving at the barriers all the interpreters in the establishment were put into requisition to explain to the Sheik the inevitableness of the preliminary shilling, but all in vain. He had neither money nor comprehension. and the G(ordian knot was at length cut by permitting him and his distinguished family to go in on credit. Thus, instead of Jew or Gentile " spoiling the Egyptians," the Egyptian succeeded in " spoiling" the royal commissioners, and the case deserves to be recorded as the first successful attempt at runnsng up a score at the Crystal Palace. Among the various proposals, the one which has appeared to receive the greatest countenance and support among per- sons of the highest eminence in science, the arts, and manufactures, in all parts of the country, as a evidenced by the numerous memorials addressed h to the Commissioners in its favour, is that b to which we have upon several occasions di-t rected public attention-viz., the establishment I t in this country of institutions conducted upon i similar principles, but varied in their details to suit the requirements of each case, to the E Conservatoire des Arts et Metiers, and Ecole Cen- trale of Paris. The following portions of the Introduction to these papers will be read with interest ," Devoted as I have been to the applied sciences, and seeking, as I have done, useful knowledge and practical experience, it has been only at a great sacrifice of time, of i money, and of advantages, that I have acquired just s0 1 much knowledge to prove to me how much more I have lost, I what difficulties have beset my path, and what incalculable i and precious advantages I mnight have obtained if such an establishment as the College of Arts and Manufactures had I been open to me with my limited means in early life. ] " At the outset, my first hope was to see a museum of arts and manufactures established from the collections of the I Exhibition, to be subservient to, and to illustrate, scientific I instruction. If the principle be good, it is quite evident that the surplus of the receipts from the Exhibition would be X totally inadequate to carry out any general amelioration of X the educational system. In the words of one of our most venerated bishops-' If that principle be true and good, it is not £200,000 that the whole nation would gladly contri- bute, but two millions if necessary, to carry out a work which would tend to the benefit of the whole empire, by the elevation of the industrial classes, in all their grades, to a higher intellectual standard than has ever before existed amongst them.' "The subject has now expanded so far beyond the grasp of my own arguments, that I hope I shall be excused in recording the opinions of a few others more deeply expe- rienced than I have been in the wants of the countlr So long back as 1836, a committee of the House of Com- mons on arts and manufactures made a report, from which the following is an extract .- "' In taking a general view of the subject before them, the committee advert with regret to the infereuce they are obliged to draw from the testimony they have received, that from the highest branches of poetical design down to the I lowest connection between design and manufactures, the arts have received little encouragement in this country. In many despotic countries far more development has been given to genius, and greater encouragement to industry, by a more liberal diffusion of the enlightening influence of the arts. Yet to us, a peculiarly manufacturing nation, the connection between art and manufactures is most important; and for L this merely economical reason, were there no higher motive, it equally imports us to encourage art in its loftier attributes, since it is admitted that the cultivation of the more exalted branches of design tends to advance the humblest pursuits of industry, while the connexion of art with manufacture . has often developed the genius of the greatest masters in design.' ,"i n 1846, the Rev. Dr. Booth, chaplain to the Marquis of Lansdowne, and formerly Principal of Bristol College, ;wrote a pamphlet on education and educational institutions, in which, introducing the subject of industrial education, he says To any one who has carefully noted the rapid progress Lof discovery, and watched the ever-varying phases of Euro- pean society, it must be apparent, that a greater change has taken place during the last 30 years than in the whole period intervening between our revolution and the close of the last continental wars. New interests have arisen-new channels of commerce have been opened-old sciences revo,- lutionized, and new ones discovered-their applications to the practical affairs of life, the true test of the valle of a o cienes in the opinion of Bacon, are numerous beyond any former precedent-and the dominion of man over the realms nof ature is more widely spread and firmly established. L" ' Thus, while the whole aspect of society has been changed -our political institutions remodelled-our coloniesmetamor- phosed from factories into empires-the rules of international law defined--the principles of internal government amelio- rated-and those which ruled our intercourse with foreign D nations abandoned-the circle of the sciences daily enlarging a -Saxon laws, manners, and religion hourly expanding the . sphere of their influence from us, as from a centre, till. it ais no longer a matter of faint hope, but of cheering proba- 3bility, that the " whole earth shall be one language, and of lone speech," if not literally at lesst actually-we find the edu-n ecation of the poorerclasses only just begun, that of the middle and upper classes stationary or retrograde, little changed from , that of which Milton expressed his condemnation.' "t Sir John Herschel draws a true picture of the times, in I saying-' Whole branches of continental discovery are un- studied, and indeed almost unknown even by name. It is tvain to conceal the melancholy truth. We are fast dropping lbehind. In mathematics we have long since drawn the rein, l and given over a hopeless race. In chemistry the case is X not much better.' " Professor de Morgan observes-' The present neglect of natural philosophy and natural history will furnish acurious lstory for after times. It will be on record that among the . first commercial people in the world, who depended for Itheir political existence on trade and manufactures, there swas not, generally speaking, in the education of their youth, s one atom of information on the products of the earth, whe- ther animal, vegetable, or mineral, nor any accotnt of the ai principles, whether of mechanics or or chemistiry, cien, .when applied to these products, constituted the distinction a | of their country. And this, when the studies so abandoned I were allowed by all to be worthy of pursuit, simply as an tI exercise of the reason, and without any reference to their f wappichtill This story will one day excite some wonder, ich will be removed when it is added, that the tone of school education was given by certain endowed establish- I meuts, which, resting their existence upon the fame ac- quired when Latin and Greek were reputed the only useful I branches of instruction, used their influence to exclude all others, long after the rational part of mankind had pro- as nounced that more was necessary.' t i "The requirements of a clever youth coming from a first- n rate school of the present day are generally that he will be I found to be tolerably well skilled in the mysteries of longs e and shorts, to have acquired a facility of stringing together doggrol verses, to have construed sconneeted seraps from |ancient writers, such as are to be found in popular selections yof extracts, his attention having never been drawn to any of e | those models of classic purity so numerous in his owi;I familiar with the genealogies niod exploits of the heathen di- a vinities ; well versed in the history of the Trojan war, and I the feuds of the Grecian heroes, and but little in the social It convulsions of his native soil, and the political storms which 1. have swept over its face ; slightly acquainted with geogra- phy ; initiated into arithmetic, not as a science built upon ee principles, but as aset of rules, the arbitrary invention (for e anything he knows to the contrary) of the bookmaker; and acquiescing upon trust in a few propositions of Euclid. Liberated from the irksome and monotonous detail of his taskmasters, he enters gladly on some professional . career-lie is placed in the office of a man of great eminence, is who has no leisure to teach his apprentices the principles of i those sciences on which his art is founded, and their appli cations to the business in hand; and even although he had, I he cannot communicate them clearly, and in logical oon- nexiou, for although he knows them, fie has not been taught them himself, but has picked them up, one here, now another, there, again, often through the blunders of him- self or others; so that, left to grope his way, it is strange indeed if the pupil ever, or at least till late in life, ac- quires a knowledge of Iia art. The young man then starts in life with the disheartening reflection, that his long years of laborious drudgery at school have been thrown away; can it be a matter of surprise, that he should look upon learning as a humbug-that hle should loathe the thoughts of Greek or Latin, having been forced to swallow their bitters and permitted to taste none of their sweets- that, loosed from control and left ih comparative freedom, the more perilous from recent restraint, without mental re- sources, the gnawing of the passions ' those vultures of the mind,' now for the first time felt-fie should waste his lei- sure hours in frivolous and unprofitable amusements ? " With such opinions, I have ventured to address the ac- companying papers. It is to such devotion to practical science that we can boast of such men as Wollaston, Davy, Herschel, ?? Brewster, and it is to encouragement of such practical education that we may look to maintain the high position and commercial prosperity we have held for so many generations. We have nov cast aside the heavy armour of protection, to wage that great commercial coniflict in which we are engaged, with limbs unfettered and with motions free. We shall require all those aids which the discoveries of modern science have placed within our reach-all that force of cultivated intellect which education in its moat perfect form can bestow-all that perseverance and indomitable energy which moral training, founded upon re- ligion, can alone create-to bear us victorious through that mighty struggle (and not the less mighty because peaceful) in which is involved the destiny of our empire. For we know of no instance where commerce has again revisited the abodes she has once forsaken. The sun will not shine in the evening where it shone in the morning; nor will 'the shadow which has gone down on the dial go backwards,' as a sign of returning health and vigour, to a people hastening to decay; or to prolong the day of prosperity for a nation whose glories are departing. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. Her Majesty, the Prince, several of the Royal children, and the Prince and Princess of Prussia again spent upwards of ; two hours on Saturday in the building. The general visitors are ; still as numerous as ever, and the receipts show a gradual and steady daily augmentation. Although the organs are labelled with promises of musical performances at stated hours, we hear little music, except from the French organ and the pianos. A large and very elegant one from Messrs. Broadwood's manufactory was placed in the English nave on Saturday, and the performances of a clever amateur or professor attracted a 'crowd of admiring auditors. The Messrs. Hunt and Roskell have just opened a very wonderful display of bijouterie and gems, which were on Saturday the great attraction of the Exhibition, and upon which we shall have something to say in detail as soon as we can procure a sight of them. We hear many complaints—and we can vouch personally for their truth—of the inattention and takes, we :suppose we must call them, of the refreshment attendants, in all three departments. We hope it is only necessary to call the attention of the caterers to the matter, but however the wealthy visitors may pass over little over-charges, or put up with a sixpenny article when they are informed the penny economic treat cannot be had, the affair will be very different in a week hence, when the working classes and artisans from the country have possession of the building, and are endeavouring by the most lengthened practicable stay to have the utmost possible value for their shilling. We propose in the present notice; to cross the line of demarcation that divides Great Britain and her dependencies and colonies from the other contributory countries, to which we have hitherto almost exclusively confined ourselves, and enter one of the most curious and interesting departments of the Exhibition—lndia. A single glance at the rich display of gold and silver and embroidery and jewels which meets the eye on either side, will inform us that we are among the traditions and the records of the past, amidst the gorgeous display of Oriental magnificence, and the somewhat profuse embellishments of barbaric splendour and tropical luxury. We are among the products of a people EC) much talked of and so little known in this country—of a people who are destined to become one day the most valuable and extensive customers for the purchase of manufactured goods, or the production of the raw material of industry; and we may premise that the display of the latter will surprise those who are unacquainted with the extent and variety of the resources of India. The first impression which the collection makes upon the observer is the vast expenditure of manual labour bestowed upon articles merely of an ornamental character. It indicates the little progress that has been made by this vast empire, in the course of centuries, in the adaptation of mechanical facilities and improved machinery; it shows also the small value of human labour in a teeming population and a tropical climate, where the neeessaries of life can be procured at a comparatively low rate; and, finally, it proves the low scale of civilisation when we find so much that contributes to regal splendour, and so little calculated to sunserve the minor wants and comforts of the bulk of the population. All that has reference to the mass of the people is rude, primitive, plain; while all that can minister to the pride and pomp of thsir rulers is gorgeously extravagant. Of this bronzed and dusky race, the great bulk of whom are ground down in hopeless and helpless poverty by the exactions of the native rulers, upwards of one hundred millions own the sovereignty of this country. It will be a glorious thing for Great Britain if she will render her mission one of peace and civilisationif she will endeavour to develope the resources which science and research have enabled her to discover, give the peaceful and industrious Hindoa remunerative employment, avert the horrors of those periodical visitations of pestilence and famine which improvidence and misrule have entailed upon those productive regions, and thus render our hold upon the supremacy of India the most solid and substantial of allnamely, that which is bated upon the affections and the good-will of the people. On the north aide of the nave, surrounded by a triple protection of iron and brass railings and plate-glass, are the celebrated Lahore Jewels, which are one resplendent blaze of large-sized emeralds, diamonds and bunches of pearls—a mass of the latter thrown carelessly on the counter is valued at 6000 guineas. A state coat is a perfect galaxy of gold embroidery and pearls, of which there are large bunches on either shoulder, in the form of epaulets, interspersed with emeralds. A girdle, in which about a dozen large squareshaped emeralds are set, surrounded with pearls, is one of the most valuable of the many costly productions in this case. Some of the emeralds, from having verses from the Koran engraved on them, are, In the eyes ot the Mahoraedan ' princes, of inestimable value, and in the East these, with the pearls, which appear to be as plentiful as berries, are the favourite gems. Hill, the antiquarian, says the emerald the same as the ancient smaragdus, and in its perfect state is the most beautiful of all gems. Tne oriental emerald is of the hardness of the sapphire and ruby, and is second only to the diamond in lustre and brilliancy. A model of a gun, the carriage and wheels of agate, and some agate and jasper boxes, set with pearls, are also displayed. At the corner, towards the transept, are specimens and models of the various craft that are common to the Indian seas, for trading; fishing, and piracy, and passing within the compartment we come to a tent fitted up in the true, or rather fabulous, eastern magnificence. Within are hung two large state elephants' trappings of crimson and green velvet, richly embroidered and fringed with gold lace. On the floor, on a similarly embroidered carpet, the King of Oude's crown, resplendent with jewels, and near this are two small silk carpets worked by the hand, upon which nobody under the rank of a nabob would venture to sit; they are valued at 50 guineas each. Ranged around the tent are curiously. carved ivory tables, inlaid with silver, the workmanship of which is the perfection of minute elaborateness. Upon these are placed a variety of figures in carved ivory, in all the beauty and delicacy for which this species of Indian handicraft is proverbial. Nothing more strikingly indicates the adaptability of the population of our vast Indian empire for education in the various departments of manufacture and the imitative arts than the display of small figures, coloured and modelled after life, and the beautiful specimens of carving, which are profusely displayed—the minuteness of detail and the delicacy of execution are perfectly wonderful, when the rough tools and primitive methods of workmanship are considered. One table is covered with a set of ivory chessman, in imitation of the antique sculptures of Nineveh; and another has a whole regiment of Indian soldiers, with their musical instruments, &c. A pair of ebony chairs have high carved backs, which, at the first glance, appear to be beautiful Berlin castings of open fretwork. A hookah in chased silver, with a purple velvet hookah carpet embroidered in silver to match, displays the vast amount of labour and ingenuity bestowed upon the decoration of this eastern luxury. Ivory canes and walking. sticks inlaid with gold and silver, and ivory ily-fans formed of ivory cut into delicate threads and others of the tail of the elk, the handles chased and inlaid with the precious metals, are among the gorgeous accessories of this eastern scene of magnificence. In a compartment behind this tent, which has not yet been opened to the public, are two large marble couches and chairs of Rajpootana marble, sculptured by natives, and intended as a present for her Majesty. An Indian state carriage, elaborately carved and gilt, and an Indian state bed, with carved silver posts and wrought silk hangings, richly decorated with gems, and valued at Ii;.JU guineas, is also to be presented to her Majesty at the close of the Exhibition. In this compartment are also some sandal-wood work and jewel boxes, the carving of which exceeds in delicacy and minuteness even the Swiss productions, and wondrous ivory caskets, inlaid with silver, in rich moresco patterns. The fibres of the cocoa nut have been, by the ingenuity of the natives, made subservient to the production of come baskets and boxes of elegant forms; and two ivory chairs, inlaid with gold, formerly belonging to the Rajah of Vizerangum, will excite the wonder and admiration of the visitors. Ranged in stalls ontsi le these gorgeous Indian productions are a collection of Indian toys and specimens of all the varieties of Indian fruit, in carved wood, coloured after nature. More interesting still is the display of all the Indian tribes and castes in their appropriate costume, and engaged at their several trades and occupations. It will afford the English visitors an opportunity of estimating the numerous retinue of servants required in an Indian household. We have the valet, the cook "frying a fowl," the pipe preparer, and all the infinite division of domestic labour. Then the trades : the barber shaving a dark man's head; two sawyers at work with a most primitive saw; a waskerman beating out clothes on a fluted board; a water-carrier, after the meneer described in the "Arabian Nights," n his leather bottles. In the Tunisian division a full-sized leather bottle, for carrying across a camel's back in the desert, may be examiued. Peasani s are shown with native machinery, putting a handful of sugar-canes between a couple of rollers turned by an ox; while, beside, are others boiling the sugar. Musicians, singers, dancing-girls, mendicants, Brahmins, the model of a European court of justice in the interior of Bengal, native religious festivals a large group of figures ann animals showing the whole process of collecting the native revenue, a complete representation of an Indian fair, with the principal buildings, modelled with the exactness of imitation for which the Hindoos are so justly celebrated. Merchants expose their wares ca mels unloaded repose o n th e re d and scorching sand, soldiers pile their arms, the juggler performs his tricks, the story-teller tells his tale, the horseman grooms his Arab steed; the elephant, with grass in his trunk, pricks up his ears as Lis master beckons to him; some smoke, som e eat, a great lord rides through in state, a fakeer or saint begs—and as the spectator looks he fancies he hears the hunt and busnle and music of the busy crowd. These pictures of Indian life and customs are extremely interesting. All are modelled by native artists, and are faithful and well -executed illustrations of the internal economy of our Indian empire. There are also models of a silk factory, a silk farm, the town and fortifications of Lahore; models of the rude and primitive looms, in which ecltton, silk, carpets, 'Sze., are won by the natives, ?f temples in carved stone, and of the Rajah and anee of Tanjore in pith, a aad silvery-looking substance from the interior of the tree, which has also been applied to the manufacture of hats. We should be glad to see them introduced into this conntry—any change from the close, black, and cumbrous English male head-dress would be welcome, and these include all the requirements of airy lightness, perfect ventilation, and shapeliness. We commend them to the consideration of the committee who have undertaken to reform our head gear. Facing the transept are one or two bays, which contain a variety of Indian dresses in silk, cotton, muslin, &c., and specimens of gold and silver cloth and embroidery. A new material, the pine-apple fibre, has been applied to the manufacture of fine cambric, as delicate-looking as cobweb, and richly embroidered in gold. An o th er d escr i pt i on of Indian tissue—the " mul-mul,' is perfectly transparent, and of such fineness that a large mass of it can be made to pass through the smallest ring. The real Indian Cashmere shawls are here exhibited in a variety of patterns and colours. They will doubtless attract the peculiar attention of the lady visitors. Their value, like that of large-sized jewels, is altogether conventional, and must be estimated by hundreds c-f pounds. It is said that to make cue of these Cashmere shawls will take a man, his wife and family, seven years ! If we were to enumerate a tithe of the glittering and costly fabrics here displayed, we should be suspected of Eastern hyperbole, cr of drawing upon an imagination wrought upon by the exhibition of so much oriental epiendour. Some of the shawls have patterns worked in bed pearle wrought into the silk, and thousands are employed in this way in the adornment of a single article of dress. The state umbrellas are stiffened with gold embroidery, have massive carved silver handles ; and everywhere there are evidences of the profuse extravagance with which the precious metals and gems are employed. On the south side of the nave, and equally well protected from the too near approach of longing eyes and itching fingers, is the second great diamond of the Exhibition, which goes by the poetic Hanle of the Darria-i-Noor, or "sea of light." Jr is set as an armlet, with several lesser gems around it, and is one cf the trophies of Indian conquest, being taken during the Sikh war. It has a flat surface, and the cutting, like that of its great compeer, "the mountain of light," is not such as to show eff the beauty of the gem to the best advantage. In this case there is also a whole tea of pearls, some of large size ; and in all the glitter of barbaric pomp are housings and bridles and saddles, etudded with large gems, all the trappings being heavy with gold lace; temples, carved in solid silver, and palatiquins and their bearers, matchlocks and spear heedies, eiepla)ing equal richness of decoration and beauty of finish. It is some relief to the eye to penetrate to the department of vege . ,able and mineral productions raw materials. Here we find models of agricultural implements, rude, but effective, and little altered in their forms during a thousand years; ma , chines for polishing jewels ; carts and waggens, with solid wooden wheels, as still used in the agricultural districts in many parts of the continent; a large collection of musical instruments, of uncouth shapes and sounds ; machines for cleansing cotton, grinding wheat, drawing water, &c. Specimens of rope made from the plantain fibre, as tough as iron; and specimens of paeer from Nepaul, as delicate as gauze. The raw materials, orce, minerals, vegetable productions, and timber, are suggestive of the vast extent of almost unexplored wealth that yet lies nearly useless in the heart of the great Indian empire. Tea from Assam and the Hinielayas; sugar, of which there are numerous specimens; coal, found in great abundance and variety; iron, the raw material of the wendroue Indian steel; tin, zinc, and other metals, are also here. Edible bird's-nests from Java, at three guineas per lb., with specimens of the nests and the birds, will suggest the idea of a new luxury to our epicures, and may probably furnish a hint for the great banquetting house over the way. In the military department are tulwars, spears, daggers, and arrows —shields of polished steel concealing four pistols behind, which can be fired by a spring; Damascus blades of the finest temper and keenest age, and models; of all the different kinds of artillery and field-pieces used in the East India Company's service. Matchlocks, swivel-mounted carved guns, the long and deadly weapon the wall gun, and complete suits of chain armour. The specimens of pottery and earthenware, and porous water jars, are numerous, and the shapes peculiar. On the sides ot the compartmee tears hung some large sized silk carpets in rich colours, which, from the quantity of the material used, and the length of time occupied in their manufacture, must be of great value. Among the numerous specimens of lamps is a large one called the peacock self-feeding lamp, taken out of a temple of the Devras or nondealers of the Suraogie persuasion. Elie oil as it is consumed trickles down from the breasts of the peacocks into the reservoir. Although this was corsieered a sacred vessel, and not even to be touched by Europeans, as soon as it was known that it was intended for the eireat Exhibition in the mother country, it was readily given up. This sketch of some of the most striking contributions it our East Indian possessions will show our readers the extent, variety, and interest of the collection, which we may add was not up to Saturday night fully displayed, and will probably he found in the course of the present week to display many other rich and canoes objects. - - --- We may here direct attention to Mr. Richard Gunter's bride cake, which is in Class 29, No. 112. This cake stands about four feet high, is sexagonal, and weighs, independent of its white sugar covering, upwards of 224 lb. Three of the six compartments of t!ie base contain bas-reliefs allegorical of the marriage of Cupid and Psyche. The mythological tableau of pure white sugar on a pink ground represent Psyche's first sight of Cupid; the marriage of Cupld and Psyche, in the presence of Jupiter Juno, Venus, Mars, &c. The last the triumph o f C u p i d and Pysclie. The remaining three compartments are devoted to the initial and cipher of the bride and bridegroom. Between each of the six compartments are infant children entwined, to represent innocence; doves surmount the infant figures which act as an ornamental relief to the e d ge o f the cake. Medallions containing allegories descriptive of the career of that most celebrated heathen deity, the God of Love, are placed round the edge alternately with shields for the heraldic arms of the contracting parties, and the arras of their respective houses. A network of white sugar covers the top of the cake, on which rest festooned vases filled with nuptial flowers. A sexaaoual column, with arabesque ornaments, rises from the centre, the projecting supports having several shields for the crests. The column is supported by a group of joyous Capids; the upper figure supporting a baket containing the orange blossom, the lily of the valley, snowdrop, &c., emblematical of youth and beauty.
