THE Daily News, in an editorial article, states, that at a solemn meeting of the Commissioners of the Exhibition, it has been determined that the Crystal Palace is to be opened in state by the Queen on the Ist of May; and that the only persons to be admitted to this ceremony are the Royal Commissioners, the diplomatic body, the Members of the Government, and of the Household. " A more impolitic, a more absurd, or a more ludicrous resolution the Commissioners could not have come to. That a mere knot of individuals, about whom, with the exception of the Queen, the Prince, and one or two Ministers, the people of England care not one farthing, should thus, like maggots in a huge Cheshire cheese, enjoy the opening of a vast national exhibition, which in itself, and in its inauguration, is not only a national but a European fele, is monstrous. That these gentlemen should enjoy the honours and privileges of a private and premature view is all very well. They may enjoy it in secret and in quiet on the last day of April, and the public will not inquire. But that upon the day which has been already announced for the first day of opening, not only the public, but even that elite of society, which could afford, and which has paid, its three guineas for season tickets—that they should be excluded, is really impertinence, to use the least offensive word. The building would contain 40,000 persons. We are quite certain that Sir Robert Peel, who was one of the Exhibition Commissioners, would never have sanctioned an anachronism so gross as this, of a mere, narrow, Court opening of the Great Exhibition." The Times also, in an editorial article, states, that all visiters, even the exhibitors, are to be excluded from the building while the Queen, attended by a score or so of Lords and Ladies-in-Waiting, shall have celebrated the opening mysteries. " The resolution of the Commissioners, which imbodies their determination of excluding the public, is now lying before us, and we here copy it verbatim, lest we should be suspeottd of an attempt to practise upon the credulity of our readers. It runs as follows:—' Her Majesty having been pleased to signify her intention of visiting the Exhibition on the occasion of its opening, on the let of May, the doors of the building will not be opened to the public on that day till one o'clock, at which hour the holders of season tickets will be admitted.' Now, what does this mean? The only possible suggestion which can occur to the mind is, that some doubt may exist in the mind of Her Majesty's advisers as to her safety, in case she should enter a building in which so many thousands of persobs are to be collected together. But where does the real danger lie? Is it within, or without the building, even admitting the preposterous idea that there is any danger at all? Is it not just as complete an affair of police regulation to take proper steps for Her Majesty's security within as without the Crystal Palace? It is of course not without great repugnance that we bring ourselves even to mentions question of this kind, but it is impossible to offer a satisfactory comment upon the resolution of the Commissioners without adverting to the probable motive upon which that resolution has been founded. If it be as we suppose, Her Majesty's advisers are leading their Royal Mistress to a course which will be profoundly unpopular, and without an adequate motive. Surely Queen Victoria is not Tiberius or Louis XI., that she should be smuggled out of a great glass carriage into a great glass building under cover of the truncheons of the police and the broadswords of the Life Guards? Where most Englishmen are gathered together, there the Queen of England is most secure! No reasonable person would ask more than;that the 6,000 or 7,000 holtlers of season tickets should be admitted to the building whilst Her Majesty is opening the Exhibition in person. The price of the ticket affords something like a guarantee that the mob would be of a select character—sufficiently so for the purpose in view. Besides, there is no reason to doubt that, in numerous instances, the season tickets were purchased on the faith that their holders would be admitted to a sight of the opening pageant. What does the number of 6,000 or 7,000 persons signify within the area of this vast building? They would scarcely be sufficient to give Her Majesty a hearty cheer, worthy of the Crystal Palace and the occasion. We trust most sincerely, on all accounts, that Her Majesty's advisers will reconsider this resolution. Better, far better would it be, to forego any public ceremonial whatso ever, than to carry it out in a form so offensive to the feelings of every Englishman." FRANCE. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. In accordance with the powers vested in the t Royal Commission, the price of the season tickets | was yesterday raised to four guineas for a gentle- s man's and three guineas for a lady's ticket; and a such is the present rapid demand for the tickets p that we apprehend, in the course of a day or two, al a further increase in price will take place, for the purpose of limiting their sale. This conduct has, ,n we understand, given dissatisfaction to some par- 6 ties; but after the statements made by us upon F1 two occasions during the last week, that it was the p intention of the Commissioners immediately to do s so, it can hardly be said to have taken the public by surprise. Those who have hitherto delayed pro- al viding themselves with tickets are the only parties I to blame in the matter. a The progress made during the last few days in ' w the completion of the arrangements of the Exhi- ft bition have been such as to render it impossible in Ir any single notice to convey to the reader any ir adequate idea of its extent. If the wand of the enchanter has been supposed to have assisted in the erection of the unique and colossal building in 1 Hyde' Park, it is not the less appropriate to sup- i pose that the same presiding genius has exerted his B. powers in the decoration and garniture of its im- M muense area. In whatever direction the eye turns, at some newly developed production of industry, or something illustrative of the wealth of nations meets the gaze. Where, yesterday, silence held ?? sway over plain deal counters, to-day has become the AccetI of ceaseless activity, which to- tir mnorrow will give place to order and beauty. The French department yeat-rday presented a rei mostextraordinary and exciting scene. Upwards of F a thousand of the exhibitors of that country were c present, for the purpose of unpacking and arranging B their goods. Though much remains to be done, there is no doubt that on the 1st of May the exposition of French industry will be one of the A most perfect and complete in the Exhibition. From cc Rome several very fine groups of statuary have been unpacked, including, among others, " Rinaldo a and Clorinda," by Rinaldi of Rome; " Cupid and Psyche," 'Fidelity," and "Gratitude;" two statues of "Nymphs," by the late It. J. Wyatt ; and a A statue by L. Macdonald. A sculpture court in the Austrian department, devoted to articles chiefly of or Italian sculpture, is now exceedingly interesting. The Zollverein may be said to have almost coln- pleted the whole of its arrangements and fittings, and its various courts promise to be exceedingly interesting and attractive, from the great variety A and value of the articles exhibited. An exceed- ingly rich display of gold and silver church plate was N restertlily added to the articles from the Zollverein. ic holland has made a gorgeous display of carpets ci and candelabra and a stomacher of brilliants, in L the centre of which is a medallion of her Majesty, is of great beauty and value. Russia shows sonlic B, very fine specimens of inlaid wood. Two porcelain Al vases, sent from the Imperial China Manufactory all at St. Petersburg, will, from the extreme richness n of their colouring and the beauty of the designs, prove exceedingly attractive ; there are several ex- quisite paintings on china from the same manufac- n tory, one of which, copied from Bergher, is a perfect L gem. There are also two large jasper vases, of large s size and immense value, the polishing of which was so effected by diamond dust. In addition to the articles i of malachite furniture previously referred to, a very c elegant sideboard, formed from the tulip wood, has fin been sent, by command of his Imperial Majesty. The United States make a very interesting and al business-like show in the galleries, of calicoes, sheeting, and printed fabrics, from the St. Law- as rence, and other manufactories in Massachusets. at We will not anticipate the opening of the Exhibi- tion by dwelling upon the valuable and interesting E articles which in a few days will be open to the 1A inspection of the public, as ample opportunities hr will be afforded us, after the Ist of May, for dis- c cussing their merits, and directing the notice of the T visitor to them. A Those who may be disposed to take the gloomy v side of the picture, and who suppose that England is to derive no benefit from the great gathering of . all nations, will be happy to learn how complete I and valuable is the collection of machinery upoti I the British side. This is all in a remarkable I state of forwardness, and awaits but the order to I turn on the steam, to start at once into life and F activity. One of the most ingeniously constructed 3! machines, and one which, at the present momnent, i is occupying a considerable degree of attention in the hosiery and woollen districts, is the circular loom of the Chevalier Claussen. This loom was yester-E day fixed in its place; and without going at pre- i sent into any of the details of its construction, or a mode of working, we may simply state that a child may with ease make with it twenty pairs of stock- a ings in a day. Any pattern may be introduced v into the fabric, by an arrangement of the most simple nature, and one which supersedes to a great E extent the use of the Jacquard loom. We were in- formed that this small machine is the only machine r worked by hand which is capable of producing a larger quantity of goods than any other single looni worked I by steau power. The number of "picks" which it can make per minute, when worked at ordinary speed, is not less than 700. In the weaving depart- meut, Messrs. Kentworthy and Bulloughs, of Black- burn, also exhibit a very fine collection of their patent power-looms. The cotton machinery of Messrs. Platt and Co. is probably unrivalled in the world. It has been got up mainly through the in- strumentality of Colonel Lloyd, one of the special commissioners who was deputed to visit the manu- facturing districts for the purpose of stirring up the somewhat dormant energies of the manufac- turers. Messrs. Platt and Co. have, we believe, i expended upwards of £5,000 in the getting up of the collection of cotton machinery. The mnanufac- turing tools and engines of Messrs. Whitworth and Co., of Manchester, are of the highest possible cha- racter. Taken as a whole, we apprehend there is no country in the world which could produce such a room of machinery. In the department of locomotives and railway carriages, prominent above all other articles is the "Liverpool," upon Crampton's patent, sent in by the London and North-Western Company, the most powerful narrow-gauge engine ever constructed. There are a number of others-" Aridl's Girdle," a small four-wheel engine ; " Little England," a small engine and tender joined together, upon six wheels; and a large one, sent in by Stephenson, having two large driving wheels behind, and six smaller ones in the front of the engine. A con- siderable number of railway carriages, first, second, and third class, have been sent in, among which is a beautiful first-class carriage, formed of polished teak bodies, and made by M1r. Williams, for the Great Northern Railway. Leaving the courts devoted to machinery, and en- tering, it will be found that in almost every depart- ment of manufacture British industry will be well represented. Considerable advance has of late years been made in our glass and porcelaine mane- factures, and it is gratifying to know that the manu-4 facturers of this particular description of goods have exerted themselves in earnest to support the credit of the country. On former occasions we nave re- ferred with pleasure to the contributions from the Potteries, and from all that we have seen we have reason to believe that Worcester will not be iiwor thily represented at the Exhibition. The principal exhibitors for that city are Messrs. Chamber- lain and Kerr, the specimens exhibited by whom are fully equal, if not superior to any ever yet produced at the Worcester facto- ries. The most handsome and artistic are the sets of honeycomb china-a tea-table service with tray -and a communion service, the latter bearing beautiful paintings of scriptural subjects. A tea service of egg-shell china, recently ordered by Ma- dame Celeste, will also form part of tile display. Vases of various elegant kinds, and pictures in medallions, fruit and cake baskets, candelabra, &c., will be shown by this firm. Messrs. Grainger have concentrated their strength, almost exclusively, upon specimens of semi-porcelaiii-though they also send a few highly-ufiished articles in china. The semi-porcelain, from its superior strength and comparative cheapness, is likely to be ge- nerally used instead of the china, which it resembles in almost every respect, except its transparency. Amongst Messrs. Gmrainger's con- tributions to the Exhibition are a ewer and basin of very elegant design ; a dejeusner ser- vice and tray of egg-sbape design, imitation honey- conmb, traced in turquoise, with leaves and ears of wheat. The most remarkable part of Messrs. Grain- ger's exhibition, however, is a small model of a re- markable font at Brook, Norwich. This is au oc- tagonal font, having in ijs upper compartnlielt61 figures, in high relief, illustrating the seven sacra- meents and the crucifixion ; and in the lower, four saints and four evangelists. It is a most intricate and beautiful work of art, and could only have been produced by dint of the greatest skill and persever- auce. The Emperor of Rtussia has decided that a commission of manufacturers and mnch of science, under the presidency of Count Kileinmichel, Director-General of Public Works, shall be sent to the Exhibition at London, and shall visit France to examine the principal manufacturing establish- ments. The Emperor has also decided that such of his sub- jects as may visit London may pass through France on under- going certain formalities. The arrivals of the last three or four days of goods from abroad for the Great Exhibition have been confined to some hundreds of packages by different steaniers from France anid Belgium, and a few packages by the steamers from Holland and the Haniseatic ports. The corps of examining officers of the revenue at the Exhibition Building has been reinforced within tie same period, in order to afford every possible facility and despatch, Ol the part of the Customs Depart- ment, for the speedy unpacking and examination of lie packages from abroad, and to prevent the least delay and inconvenience. -

We have now before us a series of reports presented to a general meeting on the 10th April, which was a special one, not only to receive from the directors the declaration of a bonus for the last quinquennial period, but the results also of one of the most searching, and, as we shall shew, one of the most useful investigations ever yet instituted by any life assurance company into the state of its affairs. Had this investigation merely resulted in a satisfactory proof that the company had attained almost unexampled prosperity, we should have contented ourselves with briefly congratulating all con- cerned in it. But the directors have manifestly had a higher object in view than merely giving with just pride an account of their past stewardship. They have, now at the conclusion of the first quarter of a century of the company's existence, tested its con- dition by the most stringent rules, estimating their resources on the very lowest, and their obligations on the very highest valuation ; and this they have done with a view of seeing whether they cannot in future safely afford to conduct the business of life assurance on more liberal principles, than it would have been prudent for them to do without the justification of an ample past experience. It is not, however, tho pecuniary position of the company alone which has led them to the conclusions which we are about to comment upon. There are other phenomena connected with life assur- ance, which reveal themselves to the ?? and dis- cerning mind, besides those which are developed by the balance-sheet. There is no branch of science so purely inductive as the science of life assurance, and none in which patient and acute observation is rewarded with so many useful suggestions and gratifying discove- ries ; and the world is now about to receive the benefit of some important truths which may be considered as fully established by the experience of the Standard. First. The Indisptilability of Policies.— -This is a ques- tion which, during the last few years, has excited much discussion, one party contending that a policy, once granted, should become ipso facto indefeasible ; a second, that it ought only to be challenged on the ground of palpable fraud ; and a third, that every life assurance company should reserve to itself the power of dealing with every emerged policy according to its own convic- tions of the merits of each case. Many very fair argu- ments can be adduced for each of these views ; but we must confess that neither of them has given us unqua- lified satisfaction. Absolute indisputability appears to us to be a temptation to fraud ; and resistance on the plea of palpable fraud, a temptation to evasion ; and unconditional power to contest the objections of a policy on grounds however trivial or technical, posi- tively unjust. We are quite aware that the boards of life assurance companies are generally inclined to behave not only honestly, but liberally; but the very fact that a policy may be disputed deprives it of its transferable character and commercial value ; while, on the other hand, the policies of a company which grants them without any reser- vation or warranty of good faith at all, must always appear to men of business, securities not to be classed Al. Now, in our opinion, the directors of the Standard have solved the problem which has puzzled us. They have resolved, that the property of indisputability shall be imparted to all their policies after premiums have been paid upon them for five years— a period of proba- tion most happily fixed upon, because, as no bonus can attach to their policies until the end of that term, few of their policies can have acquired much ready money value until then. And we approve of this arrangement for another reason. We have known cases in which lives have been fraudulently insured, because they have been consciously rotten ; but we can hardly suppose that any man, or his friends for him, would speculate upon the success of such a fraud, where the main con- dition of its succeeding is, that the rotten life must last five years. Secondly.— Residence abroad, or going without leave or license beyond limits circumscribed by the policy. We are quite sure that this stringent condition of a policy has proved more detrimental to its value as a security than even the possibility of its being disputed on the grounds of original misrepresentation, concealment, or omission. To be perfectly secure against it, the assignee of a policy should hold (ridiculous as it may seem), as a subsidiary security, a perpetual writ of ne exeat regno against the assigner. Hence we have always advocated the relax- ation of this rule of forfeiture as far as is consistent with prudence ; and here again the Standard has come forward to remove a difficulty which has long em- barrassed us. They propose to grant policies, which after the payment of five annual premiums shall be free from the disparaging condition of forfeiture altogether, but only to such parties whose avocations render it improbable that they will ever go beyond the bounds of Europe. The directors will of course judge for themselves in each individual case; and insurances without the irksome clause alluded to, as well as those which at the end of five years are to be pronounced indefeasible, are to be termed " Select Assurances." These .are two great steps towards the perfecting of the practice of life assurance, as we shall show more minutely in our next, when we shall also have to re- mark upon some other essential points iv the reports before us. — London Mercantile Journal. GREAT EXHIBITION. Monday Her Majesty and the Royal visitors went to the Crystal Palace at nine o'clock, and, as some 400 or 500 exhibitors had been formally requested to be present, more than usual interest attached to the occasion. The portion of the Exhibition marked out for inspection was the south gallery on the west side of the transept. Hitherto the noYal visits have been made in a very private manner, and, although the principal contributors were made aware that the Queen was coming, no official announcement of the fact was made to them as a body. It will be remembered that the honour of a personal inspection was promised them !.bout the time that the building was opened; and it was syemed proper, in fulfilment of that promise to give to tier Maj es ty' s grac i ous patronage o f th e Exhibition a more decided and p os iti ve c h arac t er . A c cordingly, when the Royal party presented themselves at the Crystal Palace, some 300 exhibitors were in their places ready to receive them. The public, we fear, hardly do justice to the extreme sensibilities of this class ;—jealous as they naturally are, each in his own department, for the maintenance of their several excellences, it is an extraordinary event with them to be brought face to face with the Royalty of England. Lips and tongues, that before ordinary mortals would run freely on in the labours of explanation, become confused, and falter when the Queen asks what they have to show. There were many manifestations of that kind, and one distinguished contributor, a manufacturer of warlike * weapons, too, fainted under the excitement. Her Majesty remained for two hours in the building, and during her stay conversed in the most affable manner with a great number of the exhibitors. The Times says we must again Most anxiously warn visitors not to crowd round her when her presence in the building is recognised. Though such conduct is dictated by the purest loyalty, it cannot but be disagreeable, and it is really too bad, that while the humblest person moves through the interminable • avenues of the Crystal Palace Uninterruptedly, her Majesty cannot go there without running the risk of being mobbed. Hitherto the masses of the community have stood in favourable contrast with their betters in this respect; but the experience of Monday mak e s us begin to feel doubtful even of them. If they only Opened a good broad way for the Royal party in its progress no inconvenience would be experienced, and yet all reasonable curiosity might be satisfied. The receipts at the doors Monday amounted to £2,129, and the number of spectators who entered the building was from 45,000 to 50,000. The crowds who thronged the Exhibition approached nearer the ideal upon which the scale of shilling admissions 'Was fixed than anything that we have yet witnessed. The mass was well leavened with the unmistakable _traces of a labouring population; it was at once interesting and gratifying to observe how, after a short time spent in simple Wonder and astonishment, each seemed by a natural instinct to betake himself to those departments upon which he could bring his own practical knowledge most distinctly and intelligibly to bear. On Tuesday the attendance of the public at the Crystal Palace was again immense. The number of those who paid the shilling admission fee was 48,302, and besides these there were present the season ticket holders and exhibitors and attendants. Simultaneously with the operation of the reduced rates of admission, the Executive Committee have issued a Popular Guide to the Exhibition, price twopence. In this guide (a small quarto of 32 pages) is included a plan of the building, with a general account of the arrangement of the objects exhibited;. directions for inspecting them with most advantage, and much local information, irnnortant on visiting a structure so extensive as the Crystal Palace. The appearance of the Crystal Palace on Wednesday 'was gay and striking in the extreme. It was quite full by one o'clock, and very warm in the nave and transept, but a short journey to one of the side courts was all that was necessary to secure a comfortable temperature. The anticipatory prints, in which the costumes of various nations Were contrasted, begin now to be realised by actual experience, as one jostles at every turn against a Nubian, a Turk, a Persian, or a Chinese. A superficial observer Would iay that the working classes have not yet begun to assemble; but a little attention to the various provincial dialects, and homely though sensible observations which are heard at every turn, convinces one that they are there in myriads, but that in addition to being the best behaved and most orderly, they are also the best dressed " people " in the world. It is recorded of the Emperor Alexander that on beholding the well dressed thousands assembled at a review in Hyde-park, in 1814, he exclaimed,—" But Where's the people." What would be his reflection if he saw the crowds of 1851 at the Crystal Palace? The number of admissions on Wednesday exceeded 55,000. On Thursday rather more than 50,000 persons visited the building. The amount received was—for season tickets, £lB 18s.; at the doors, £2,566 175.; total, £2,585 15s. It is stated that the Corporation of the City of London Intend to give all the clerks at the Mansion-house and the Guildhall, and also all the officers in their service, an opportunity of visiting the Crystal Palace. For this purpose they have resolved to give them all a holiday in turn, and to present each of their clerks with a guinea in lieu of a ticket of admission. Some of the private establishments of the Metropolis, where numbers of clerks and assistants are engaged, are generously emulating the munificence of the civic corporation in this matter. THE GREAT EXHIBITION S/11,—Your paper of yesterday contains an account of the arrangements that are being very properly made for extra English services during the period of the Great Exhibition. An important meeting ol the Royal Commission, which was very fully attended, took place on Tuesday in the Crystal Palace, and was presided over by Prince Albert, who was naturally anxious to see certain questions satisfactorily solved which pressed for a decision before his departure to the Highlands. All matters that could staud over, such as tbe fate of the build- ing, and tlie appropriation of the surplus funds, are still in reserve; but the following is a summary of the points iinally settled: — " The Royal Commissioners have fixed Saturday, tbe llth of October, as the day for closing the Exhibition to the public. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The building was by no means crowded on Saturday last, although the fineness of the d.y it was anticipated would assemble a large number of persons. Most of those present were season ticket-holders, and it is now pretty evident that the limit of those disposed to pay 53. for a single visit has been reached, and that the Saturday visitors will for the remainder of the period during which the Exhibition remains open be almost exclusively confined to those who have possessed themselves of the privilege of a general entree. Up to five o'clock there were not more than 12,000 or 13,000 persons present, and the great majority of these furnished no contribution to the gross receipts of the week; which have, nevertheless, been considerable. Her Majesty, his Royal Highness the Prince Albert, the King of the Belgians, and some of the junior branches of both families were at the building long before the doors were opened to the public, and spent considerable time in viewing the collection of hair, fur, and skins in the English department. They afterwards visited the leather and saddlery department, and the boots, shoes, &c., the recent improvements and inventions in all of which were described by the exhibitors. After viewing the adjoining objects in the nave, including the very handsome model, in Ladyshore terra cotta,of Lever. bridge Church, the Royal party proceeded to the cotton and other fabrics near the western entrance, and examined the extraordinary specimens of fine spinning of cotton thread. Her Majesty expressed her admiration of the extraordinary mechanical ingenuity displayed in drawieg out cotton thread to the extent of 2000 miles to the lb.; and Mr. Besley, one of the Royal commissioners, who is an extensive Manchester manufacturer of cotton, had the honour of explaining to the Royal party the machinery by which it is effected. The collection of carriages and other vehicles was then minutely inspected, and after two hours devoted to the examination of these different branches of manufacture, the Royal party left. During their visit they were attended by Mr. alke, Mr. Cole, and Colonel Reid. Her Royal Higlinesg the Duchess of Kent and suite, at a later period of the day, paid a visit to the building, and was shown through the machinery by Mr. Hensman. The Royal Princesses were also taken through the machinery by Mr. Cole and Mr. Biddle, and were much interested in the explantions afforded them of the flax machinery, Whitwortn's machinery, the beautiful display of mineral manufactures, and the furs and skins. These almost daily and protracted visits of the Royal family evince the deep interest taken by them in the success of the Exhibition, the popularity of which, established by the magnificent regal inauguration, is maintained and supported by the Royal patronage it has since received, and which will be fittingly consummated and crowned in the distribution of the prizes and medals by her Majesty in person at the close of the season. In the area appropriated to mining and mineral products there is a collection of granitic specimens from different parts of the country that serve admirably to illustrate the purposes to which this description of rock is adapted. Granite is composed of mica, felspar, and quartz, in distinct crystals, or else filling interstices between crystals, with the occasional addition of other minerals; and wherever we look around us we may see proofs of its usefulness and durability in the numerous buildings for the erection of which recourse has been had to this material. London and Waterloo Bridges, the Royal Exchange, and the British Museum, are but a few amongst the many public structures that are built of granite; and the streets of London and of most other towns are paved with it. At the Exhibition we have blocks of all kinds from Dunleary, in Ireland, Peterhead and Aberdeen, in Sco:land, Hooe Lake and Dartmoor, in Devon, and a rich and varied display from Constantine, Z-nnor, Paul, Rosemorran, Polkannygo, Carnsew, and Lewarmick, in Cornwall, the whole of which county abounds in this valuable and important rock. This material is susceptible, too, of receiving a highly polished surface, as is apparent by the magnificent specimens before u , . That from Hooe Lake, near Plymouth, is sure to strike the visitor by its polished and handsome graining, which imparts to it much the appearance of marble. To the uninitiated it is hardly conceivable that the white China clay, on or close to the same stand, and for which tbere is so large a demand in the Potteries, was at one time itself part of a mass of granite. But such is nevertheless the fact. There are certain kinds of granite, especially in Cornwall, which are undergoing rapid disintegration and decay, in consequence of the joint action of air and water upon that portion of the rock which is termed felspar. It is thus that the celebrated Cornish clay is produced: and the district in which the Carglaise Mine. at St. Austell, is situated is an excellent and characteristic specimen of decomposing granite. Whilst referring to this material we may as well direct attention also to the specimens of granite displayed at the western end, on the outside of the Exhibition Building, as suggesting by their magnitude the immensity of the geological formation out of which they were hewn. One is a solid piece of granite from Lamorna, near Penzance, in the shape of an obelisk, and the height of it is 24 feet 8 inches, and its weight 21 tons; the other is also a solid block, and forms the base of the obelisk. It was dug out of the:Carnsew quarries, near Penryn, is nearly 12 feet square, and weighs 31 tons. In this department, at No. 225 1 will be found some very interesting specimens of the se: °stances which recent discoveries have shown are to be extracted from bog peat. The west of England, Sr,otland, and especially Ireland, abound in peat; but up to a late period about the only uses to which it had been applied were as fuel and manure. The chemist has, however, stepped in, and by experimental analysia satisfactorily proved that it possesses intrinsic qualities, which constitute it a most valuable raw production, and which are likely to render it ultimately a source of employment to the labourer, and profit to the capitalist. After undergoing a certain preparation peatscharcoal acts as a powerful and completely effective deodoriser and fertiliser, and is daily coming into more general demand and favour by virtue of these qualities. And, in the mineral department of the Exhibition, along with some specimens of Dartmoor peat, may be seen various other products which are derived from it. These have been prepared by Mr. Robert Oxland, of Plymouth, and comprise acetate of lime, sulphate of ammonia, tar, pyroxilic spirit, chloroform, platine, heavy oil, and solution of caoutchonc in platine. We observe that in the same class a considerable number of sands and earths are shown, and amongst them Mr. Morrison, the agent of Earl Somers, has a specimen of sand from Reigate-heath, which is said to be highly valued on account of its fine sharp grit in the manufacture of glass. There are also specimens of the beautiful silver sand which exists in such abundance in Tunnel and Castle Caves, Reigate, and at Alum Bay, in the Isle of Wight. And not the least interesting article in the collection is the glass vase, containing 64 shades of coloured sands, which have been so arranged by Mr. Claxton, of Ventnor, as to represent several pretty figures and devices. STOVES, VENTILATING GRATES, &c.-The num- ber of stoves and heating-apparatus contributed both by English and foreign exhibitors, to the Great Exhibition, is very censiderable, but theymay allbe resolved into two kinds, those that give out heat by-conduction, and those that dis- tribute it by radiation. Open fireplaces are of the latter kind, and a considerable loss of heating power is the conse- quence of such an arrangement. Waste of fuel, unequal distribution of heat, cold currents near the floor, the pro- duction of smoke and dust, and danger to life and property, ire amongst some of the evils which are more or less ia- separable from open fireplaces. To remedy these objections to some extent, Count Rumford suggested the register stove. This was no doubt a great improvement upon the old open 6himuny, but still it did not remedy the defect to which all open fireplaces are liable. The close stove was a great improvement, and of this the close Dutch stove is the simplest example that can be produced. One of the greatest improvements in stoves of this descrip- tion is the adaptation of such a form as allows the heat to distribute itself by radiation throughout the room, instead of permitting it to waste itself by going up the chimney. Messrs. Jobson and Co., of Sheffield, have exhibited a patent stove, which not only reflects the heat from the surface and sides, but from below, the ashpit being so contrived as not to interfere with the lower part of the reflector. Messrs. Benham and Sons, of Wigunore-street; Messrs. Deane, of London-bridge; the Messrs. Gray, of Edinburgh; and Messrs. Evans, of King William-street, are also exhibitors of stoves in which the most recent improvements have been brought to bear, with a view to the utmost economy of fuel combined with the greatest heating power. Messrs. Nor- sairn and Co., of the Albion Works, Birmingham, and 131, Regent-street, have exhibited a very ingenious in- vention of this kind. By a simple contrivance a continuous stream of heated air is reflected through the apartment, and by a reverse motion the vitiated atmosphere is carried off. An equable temperiture is secured by a con- trivance which allows the air to escape, not only up the chimney from the lower part of the room, but also from the upperpart. In order that the apartment should not be overheated, a double action valve is placed atthe lower part of the fireplace, by means of which the hot and vitiated airisthrown off. One of the peculiarities of this con- trivance is that the fire is contained in an iron case from three to four feet high, which does not touch the chimney, thus leaving a hollow space outside for the reception of the soot. Cleanliness is insured by the employment of a move- able ash pan, projecting a considerable distance from the fire, and independent of the fender. But itmust be owned that although the English stoves are wvell contrived for utility and economy, they do not posses the variety of form and elaborateness of design which are displayed in some of the stoves in the Austrian and French departments. In the department allotted to Denmark is a new machine for comporeng and distributing type, which we incidentally noticed in referring to the contributions of that country. We have since been favoured by M. C. Sorensen, the inventor, with a dsscription of the machinery by which these operations are effected. Its ncvelty consists in the two operations being carried on at the same time—the composing part being supplied will tepes by the distribution of those previnsly used. For this purpose the distributing part of the machine has its place over the composing part. It rests with its hollow axis on the projected central axie of the latter, and distributes the types by revolving on that axis, every type being conducted during the revolutions to that place in the lower part of the machine to which it belongs. the lewer, or cerueosing, part of the machine the types are piled on and between reds or brass b irs, of which there are as many as there are letters, characters, or signs, wanted for printing. These rods are perpendicularly fixed between two plates of metal, in circular order, so that they form an open cylinder. The distributing part of the machine has a similar construction, consisting of vertical rods of the same size, of a temiler number, between similar circular plates. The issential difference between them is, that the one is fixed, while the other is moveable. All the rode have a longitudinal projection, by means of which the types, having corresponeiret incision, can be fixed, and slide up and down; the triangular form ef the projection and the incision keeping them in the horizontal position in which they are piled on the rods. In the composing cylinder the triangular projection on each rod ceases at the lower extremity, so that the undermost type upon it can be pushed from its ; place by the action of a spring, which is moved by a string, in connection with a scale of keys corresponding to the letters or characters. By touching the key a type is moved forward and fails, in the same position which it had on the rod, into a funnel; and on the inclined plane of this it slides down into a spiral tube, which brings of necessity all the types to a narrow opening connected with a receiver, in which the line, by type after type, is formed. By means of a common pedal, the compesed line is continually moved forward, so as to leave an open space for each succeeding type; and when the line has attained a certain length, it is removed, and a new receiver is placed at the end of the opening. The lines thus succeesively formed are afterwards divided into shorter ones, tsuielble to the width of the proposed page. If the composnor finds in the MS. words requiring peculiar types, he indicates the place by a particular sign, and the required types are supplied when the continuous line formed by the machine is divided into the shorter ones suited to the page. The inventor states further that this c imposing operation is effected its the time which in the ordinary method is required for the distribution only. To effect the dis.ribution the types must be cast expressly for the machiee, every letter or character having an incision of a different kind, corresponding with openings in a circular metal plate called the distributing plate. The ininntor then notices the various objections that may be urged, acknowledging at the same time that the machine has not yet been tested by experience. After remarking upon the objections which have been raised to every invention calculated to lessen the amount of manual labour, he concludes by observing that "it is desirable in the present progressing period that this invention, which ennobles the tedious act of cotupoiing, should meet a favourable reception and a fair trial from the enlightened body of printers and compositors in this great country, where all usenil improvements are apprec ated by a generous and intelligent public." We know not wnether the recent unfortunate catastrophes with ball,ons will stimulate the public to further experiments in that directien or render them more unpopular, but a new invention has come into the field, a model of which will he found in the western gallery, in which the assistance of the air, combined with the safety of terra firma, is put forward as its peculiar advantage ever the more aspiring but more dangerous mode of locomotion. It is termed the chervolant, or kite carriage, the vehicle being impelled by the air acting upon large kites, at the rate of 20 to 25 arles an hour. The shape may vary, but for what is termed the pilot, or uppermost kite, the common circularheaded shape is the best. The first peculiarity of this invention is, that the kite is made to fold up, the standard is divided into two equal lengths, the wings also have hinges or joints at the top; and the frame is covered with strong linen—two lines are used for what is termed the belly-band, the upper one stationary or fixed, the under one, termed the lower brace line, reeves throneh an eye in the upper line, at about the distance where the usual bow is tied in the belly-band of the common kite. Both these lines are continued down to the hand of the controller, bat enclosed in a casing of canvas or webbing. By straining on the lower brace, the kite is brought up against the wind into full action; by slackening the same, the kite is laid inactively upon the wind; thus its power is instantly increased or lessened while floating in the air. By the same means the kite is elevated or lowered at pleasure, soaring or sinking in proportion the angle is formed on the kite's surface. Another branch of this system consists of the application of two side lines, one attached to the right hand extremity of the kite, and the other to the left. By pulling the right hand line, an obliquity is given to the kite's surface on which obbquity the wind acting, the kite veers instantly to the right hind; straining on the left hand brace, the action ia directly vice versa. By this movement the traverse is performed; trees and other obstecles avoided, and many advantages obtained. The power of a kite twelve feet high, with a wind blowing at the rate of 20 miles in an hour, is as as a man of moderate strength can stand against. With a rather boisterous wind, such a kite has been known to break a line capable of suspending a weight of 200 lb. This kite spreads a surface of 49 square feet. It should be particularly noticed that these may serve as standing ratios, from which, by the rule of proportion, the power of larger kites can be calculated. Two kites, one 1.5 feet in length and the other 12 feet, have sufficient power to draw a carriage with four or five persons, when the wind is brisk. "Whit-Monday. — At nine o'clock, or thereabouts, omni- buses, cabs, and caravans filled with happy holiday folk might be seen passing in dense columns along all the leading thoroughfares towards Hyde Park ; the streets gave indications of an immense influx of visitors, and even the precarious elevation of the " knife boards" was fully occu- pied. Rain began to fall, and all tbe indications of a damp disagreeable day were realised. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. On Wednesday the temporary entrance for carriages of every description was closed to enable the flooring of the building to be completed; and on the following day a rather numerous train of people found insurmountable obstacles between their wagons and the main avenues. Most of them by other appliances succeeded in getting their goods in. • The arrangements for the display of goods are now quickly advancing. The Americans are "going ahead" in earnest, and in the French, Belgian, and Austrian compartments continuous efforts are being made. In the central passage a very fine equestrian group has been erected a mounted horse attacked by a tiger—a copy of one in bronze, in front of the Berlin Museum—executed by Herr Kiss, of Berlin. A colossal lion in bronze, from Bavaria, is also in the central avenue. The Executive Committee have issued a notice, that packing cases must be re • moved on or before the 10th of April. Saturday, an immense number of agricultural implements were forwarded. The Emperor of Austria intends to exhibit a magnificent carved book-case (containing a quantity of unpublished national music of the 15th century) which he will afterwards present to the Queen. Several intending exhibitors have invited a private view of their contributions prior to removal from their own premises. Two china dessert services, manufactured at Colebrook Dale for the Great Exhibition, have been inspected, at Messrs. Daniell's, of New Bond-street, by numerous visiters. Both are of elegant design and workmanship ; but the chief interest attaches to the revival, in one, of the rose tint introduced about 1740, and known as the "Rose Dubarry,"—which Mr. Marryat pronounces to be the most beautiful discovery in Sevres china. The excessive difficulty of its perfect production soon caused its disuse; and the present sample is understood to be the first in which this tint, at once delicate and of a deep creamy richness, is revived. Various attempts have been made of late years to revive this precious tint, but it was found impossible to diffuse it evenly over the surface of the article ; and it has been reserved for the manufactory at Colebrook Dale to solve the problem. A comparison of an old specimen with the dessert-service justifies the eminent manufacturers in claiming the credit of producing greater smoothness and uniformity of colour. In fact, it surpasses in evenness of tone the best specimens of the original artists. The softness and depth of the glaze deserve notice; and the design, in which a groupe of dolphins plays a conspicuous part, is remarkably bold and felicitous. Altogether it is a co.n-plete triumph of English art, and will probably meet with no rival from the most celebrated establishments of Europe. It has already found a purchaser in a nob,e and distinguished patron of the fine arts. The other ' service, which has also been manufactured at the Colebrook Dale Works, has been designed for the bead of a noble family of historic name. It is remarkable for the richness and elaborateness of its design ; the fruit dishes being embossed on the reverse—a novelty which demonstrates the great progress which has been made in this department. The gold decorations and chasing are of peculiarly excellent workmanship, and the armorial bearings of the noble house for which the service has been ordered are cleverly introduced. Messrs. Hunter, the eminent cabinet-makers of Moorgate-street, will exhibit a splendid Sideboard of flue English walnut tree, supported on two cornucopias and dolphin's heads, which are richly carved with fruit, flowers, and bacchanalian heads, representing youth and old age. In the centre of the back is the head of Bacchtus, indicative of full maturity, surmounted with the palm, on which is inscribed " possunt qllia posp , videntur ;" the vine, hop, and oak flow in clusters, with the hound and wild boar on each side, emblematical of the chase; a beautiful marble slab, from Galway, forms the table part. The splendid cellaret under, is per. fectly unique in design, and, when complete, will be equal in execution ; as also are two chairs, of studied structure and varied form, harmonising with the other pieces. These elaborate and beautiful specimens of English carved work have been done upon the premises of Messrs. Hunter, and are equal, in every respect, to the finest specimens of ancient or modern workmanship that we have ever seen. Two elaborate pieces of workmanship are to be contributed by Messrs. Holland and Sun, upholsterers Marylebone-street, St. James's. The first is a book case, made to form orle end of a room. The material is walnut, richly and minutely carved. In the centre is a cavity for a fireplace, of red Mona marble, with a green dragon fitted in it. Over the fireplace are three niches, with green and red marble foliage panels. At each side of these niches is a space for books, with brass doors, lined with crimson velvet. Beside each of these doors is a pedestal for statuary. Behind these are piastres exquisitely carved, representing the vine-stem and grapes, and boys with baskets gathering the grapes. At the base are snakes, and lizards, and dragons, with some of which boys are having contests; and on the stem are birds, butterflies, moths, and lizards. Under these pedestals are panels inlaid with green and red marble, and bosses of red marble. The whole is surmounted with a pediment, which is also minutely carved. The other piece is a console table and glass, with mirrors so , arranged as to represent a sheet of water, at the edge of which are the water lily, the lotus, anti the bullrush, and children playing on horns, kettle drums, and other instrutnehts, all gilded in variegated gold. Messrs. Thorne and Co., of New Bond street, have exhibited some interesting goods, manufactured in gutta perch°, and amongst them are various elegant designs intended for exhibition in the Crystal Palace. Of these the most attractive are a looking-glass and a console table, each consisting of an extremely elegant device, which probably could not have been brought to the same state of perfection by the use of any other material. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. From a comparative decline last week in the amount of visitors to the Crystal Palace since it was really opened to the public-a fact chiefly attributable, however, to the great heat of the weather-the numbers have again reached the utmost limit of accommodation. The attendance on Mon- day was one of the fullest of the season, the return exhibiting a list of 61,670 persons, amongst whom,-for the first time since the opening of the Exhibition,-there were no fresh seasou-tichet holders; that list was a blank, but the general receipts were 2,8521. 2s. The great shilling public had it almost all to themselves, there being but very few titled persons noticed among the visitors. Prince Albert was present for an hour or two in the morning, accompanied by one gentleman, but so quiet and unobtrusive was his visit that he escaped general recognition. To make up, how- ever, for the absence of English haut ton there were troops of visitors from almost every part of the civilised world,. and a vast body of our own working classes, principally from the provinces. The boys of the Naval Asylum, Green- wvich, steamed up to Chelsea in the Ariel, and, forming on the terrace, marched to the Crystal Palace, preceded by their band, and with colours flying. These juvenile heroes had hit upon an admirable plan for recovering any stray boys who might lose themselves in the vast avenues. The main body was accompanied by the cornet l piston of the band, who, every time he came to a prominent part of the gallery, or nave, struck up a flourish which soon brought all the wanderers about him, but very much astonished such visitors as had not seen the plan of the campaign. There was also a large party of naval cadets from the Norwegian corvette Ellida, now lying at Sheerness. These young gentlemen were accompanied by an interpreter, and marched through the building with a sedate gravity almost as striking as that for which English middies are so remarkable. The other naval contingent consisted of the boys of the Ven- geance, 84, now under orders for the East Indies. The men of several large establishments in London were present, the most conspicuous being a body of 500 from the great printing-office of Messrs Clowes, the printers of the vatalogue. It was understood that these men had been treated by their employers without any deduction from their wages for the day lost. The excursion trains were also numerous, and poured vast numbers into the Crystal Palace. One from Hull brought up 1,000, among whom was a Hull Exhibition club, consisting of 100 members, who came in a body, headed by the mayor, and with a distinctive flag flying. There was another Exhibition train, from Swindon, which brought up a large detachment; but indeed, to judge from the variety of dialects, Epglish, Scotch, and Irish, which resounded through the building, eveiy corner of the three kingdoms must have contributed to swell the crowd. Now that excursion trains begin to be in fall operation, and when the industrial classes are daily flocking in large num- bers to London in order to see the wonders of the Exhibi- tion, we think it right to remind them of an establishment called " the Eanelagh Club," formed under the auspices of the Royal Commission, and capable of providing at a mar- vellously cheap rate comfortable accommodation for a thou- sand persons. This club is situated on the north bide of the river, close to Cubitt's pier, and at a distance of about one mile from the Exhibition. It is provided not only with clean and well-ventilated dormitories lit with gas, and securing perfect privacy to their occupants, but there are also a dining roolm, a news-room, a lavatory, a barber's shop, and a smoking-room, all of a size which it was confidently expected that the business of the place would render requi- site. The charges are drawn ul on the lowest remunerative scale, a night's lodainc being only is., and provisions being supplied at fixed prices. We understand that those who have hitherto taken up their abode here have been much pleased with the accommodation provided for them. On Tunesday there was-as the auctioneers say-a considerable advance upon the last offer, the number of visitors reach- ig close upon 66,000, and the amount taken at the doors was 3,1091. 5s., which, with the sale of one lady's season ticket, made the sum received for the day 3,1711. 7s. Of the above number no less than 52,260 had passed the doors before one o'clock, being the greatest number, up to thlat hour, that had been admitted on any day since the opening. This last amount was particularly noted by the officials, as indicating the nmeber of new comers, the later admissions beina considered to consist more or less of the 'Vasit c5s of the place. As on the preceding day, there were vast numbers from the provinces, and the influx of foreign- ers w'as quite remarkable. The interior w'as a perfect Blabel ior diversity of tongues, and at three o'clock looked ike avast tavein-every form and citting place, even in the most conspicuous situations, being occupied by parties of various numbers, discussing the contents of their baskets with the most perfect nonchalance. And this, too, without any diminution in the business of the vdrious refreshment tables, the daily sales at which are almost incredible. One of the proprietors admitted recently to having opened 700 dozen of gingerbeer and soda water in one day; and as for ice, the demand would exhaust Wenham Lake. Whoever may ultimately benefit by the GreatExhibition, the restect- rants will have secured a pretty harvest before all is over. At present their profits are estimated by cautious calculators at 1001. a day, with every probability of a continuous in- crease. Her Majesty visited the Exhibition early in the morning, but stopped only a short time, merely promenad- ing through the machinery room, and bestowing a passing glance at the objects in the nave. The visit was quite pri- vate, and none of the executive committee were in attend- ance. Several schools, both town and country, came in vans, the most conspicuous being the Foundling Hospital children, male and female, of whom sixty, attended by their teacher, were treated to a lengthened inspection. The presence of charity chifdren in great numbers is becoming more and more one of the most remarkable fea- tures of the Exhibition; and their conduct is such as to re- flect the highest credit on the institutions to which they belong. There was also the usual detachment of the Coldstream Guards to enjoy the liberality of their colonel. Many of the provincials, especially the elder ones, were quite studies for costume, the coats, although fresh as if sent home the previous day, being evidently the work of tailors of a previous generation, and exhumed from a long sleep in trunks and drawers to honour the world's gathering. There were also many stalwart Highlanders from the far north in kilt and philabeg of the genuine grey plaid, and not the many-coloured theatrical tartan, which is only a modern innovation. Some of those visitors were models in their way. At Hunt and Roskell's splendid case of plate, there was a great crowd, and the confusion was very much increased by a game at cross-purposes played by the policemen at opposite corners: one insisted that the crowd should "pass on"' one way, while the other was equally obstinate in sending them in an opposite direction, and the consequence was, that they were constantly meet- ing in the centre, and stopping up the passage completely. It is to be observed, that wherever the police interfere activelv with the cir- culation, an immediate congestion is the consequence, while, when the people are left to themselves, they get on as comfortably as could be expected in such a crowd. The only main who seems to under- stand the marshalling of the eager sight-seekers is a little foreigner who stands at the entrance of the Milan sculpture room, and who, with a graceful wave of his hand, moves the most obese visitors about with wonderful celerity.-A return has been made of the sums re- ceived for the use of the public conveniences and lavatories, which shows in the most striking manner the complete success of the plan of the committee appointed by the Council of the Society of Arts, for establishing accommodations of this character upon a self-supporting system. We understand that the Council, in pursuance of the reconm- mendation of the committee, have leased three houses in the Strand and Fleet street, which it is intended to fit up as model establishments of this character. We would recommend respectable shopkeepers, and others possessing suitable premises in public thoroughfares, to con- sider the propriety of at once placing themselves in communication with the committee, for the purpose of co-operating in the supply of a want long felt by the public at large. By the return to which we have adverted, we find that the receipts for the " retiring rooms " and "lavatories" have been in daily-increasing progression, since the opening of the Exhibition; on the 1st of May, one shilling and six- pence was the whole amount received for these conveniences; and 6n the 30th of June there were taken 161. 2s. lid. for the retiring rooms, and 5!. 16s. Id. for the lavatories: the respective totals in each case being 4601. 16s. 2d., and 101l. 2s. 51d. The morning was sultry and lowering, and shortly after mid-day a thunder-storm rattled loudly over the transparent roof; but the human tide felt no check, and the interior was as gay and as crowded as ever. Immense numbers came from the country, and at every turn one met long trains of labourers with some distinctive badge, or troops of charity children, decently and neatly clad, and proceeding leisurely through the building under the careful guidance of their teachers. Among the country visitors were a body of 150 labourers and their families from Osborne, for whom her Majesty had been graciously pleased'to order a special steamer from the island, and a special train from Southampton, defraying all expenses until the party returned to their homes. 'THE GREAT EXHIBITION. To-MORROnW week the Crystal Palace will be thrown open-the great world fair commenced-and a sight to which history affords no parallel, displayed before an assemblage equally unparalleled-the Queen of Eng- land, surrounded by the elite of her subjects and the representatives of all the nations of the earth. The triumphs of human intelligence, from every cor- ner of the earth, from every nation, and -almost every city, will be exhibited before spectators as various in their origin. It is the first union of the world's inhabitants for one object, and of their represen- tatives in one place, since their dispersion on the plain of Shinar; and the moral union of art, intelligence, and industry, is happily typical of the change wrought out in the progress of ages, from the union of ignorance and impious presumption, that led to the confusion of tongues, and the separation of kindred. We are not of those who look with apprehension to this wonderful oc- casion, either as a godless repetition of the examples of human audacity, which Scripture records with their ac- companying chastisement, or as a, heedless exposure of the country to contagion fronm all the evils-physical, moral, and political-which foreign nations can import among us. The self-idolatry displayed on the occasions where the wrath of Heaven has been manifested as a punishment for human presumption, in whic:h some mnelancholy-minded individuals seek a parallel for the great gathering, had little in common with it in the generous spirit ; brhleh it-has its origin. And .as for the other sources f apprehenslo; we trust there-will be little occasion to dread either the plarues of the East, or the socialism of the West, or even the famine that cer- tain lugubrious fancies seem to predict, as if the ex- pected visitors were not only like the locusts of Egypt, to eat up every green thing, but to leave our granaries empty, and the vegetable and animal kingdoms both desolate. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. No better testimony can be offered to the excellence of that portion of the Exhibition which is devoted to the display of agricultural implements, than the absorbing interest with which it is regarded by gentlemen from the different corn-growing countries of continental Europe. This department is, in truth, at once an apt illustration of inventive genius and manufacturing skill, and of the superior intelligence, energy, and perseverance of our agriculturists, who, in the face of difficulties, natzra' and artificial, which ars altogether unknown in the countries referred to, have made such rapid advances in the improvement of the culture and management of the soil. Very many of the articles have been adjudged prizes at the annual meetings of the Royal Agricultural Society, and at the meetings of various local , societies. They come, therefore, to the Exhibition accompanied by a prestige which no merely experimental I machinery could possibly enjoy, and with all the improve- I ments in details which extensive use may have suggested. The application of steam to numerous farming purposes for which previously manual and horse power only was resorted to is of very modern date, and has been attended by I the best results. It is estimated that where the occupier does not avail himself of steam nearly one-fifth of the whole produce of his land is consumed by the horses employed in its cultivation. Obviously, therefore, it must be a matter of prime importance to the farmer if he can be furnished with the means for diminishing this expensive item in his annual outlay. And in the steam-engine he has them without doubt. Where coals are 20s. a ton corn may be thrashed; chaff, mangold, and turnips cut; beans, peas, and grain crushed; timber sawed, and many other operations performed by one of Messrs. Garrett's steamengines, for instance, at less than one-sixth the cost of horses. The main obstacle to the general adoption of the steam-engine is, however, that its purchase involves so large an outlay in the first instance as from 2001. to 250/.; but even this difficulty is one that may easily be surmounted, and we are acquainted with cases in which a speculative capitalist has purchased one or more for the use of a whole district, and lent it at a charge which still leaves a considerable saving to those who avail themselves of its services, whilst a fair profit is returned to the party who has made the investment. It is not an uncommon thing, either, to find several neighbouring occupiers forming a joint fund, and purchasing an engine which they use in rotation, and thus by their united action securing advantages which they would never have attained by their single and unaided effort. No agricultural visitor to the Exhibition will fail to admire the peculiar adaptability to the purposes mentioned above of the engines shown by Nlessrs. Garrett, of Saxmundham, Messrs. Clayton and Shuttleworth, of Ipswich, and other manufacturers. We annex a short published description of Garrett's engine, to which the first prize of 50/. was - awarded at the Royal Agricultural Society's Exhibition at Norwich in 1849: "The boiler of this engine is constructed with fire-box and tubes, giving a large heating surZace expo-ed to the fire, generating steam quickly, with a small quantity of water and an equally small quantity of fuel, not more than 10Ibs. Per horse-power per hour. The smoke funnel is so placed fer safety and convenience between the driving wheel and furnace door, and the waste steam is made to pass through it, so that there is no danger of ignition from sparks, or lighted matter in the smoke, which by this means are extinguished before they can possibly escape. The boiler is also covered with a jacket of non-conducting material and that cased with iron or wood, which will be found very advantageous in retaining and economising the heat when standing at work during cold weather in exposed situations. The engine is made upon the most approved cylinder and metallic-piston principle, and fitted with steam cocks, gauge cocks, safety valve, governor, and other requisites. The pump used for forcing water from the cold water cistern to the boiler is not turned off when not required, but is always kept at work; a three way cock of novel construction being provided, by which the water when not required, for the boiler is conducted back again into the cistern. By this arrangement the liability of the pipes to burst is obviated, and the pump not so likely to get out of order as when used only at intervals. A farther great advantage is obtained by the water being heated without cost in its passage from the cold water cistern to the boiler, and is frequently injected at boiling temperature. The whole is mounted on a carriage with four wheels, and may be easily turned round and removed from place to place with two or three horses." Of late years, particularly since he has entered upon so keen a race of competition with the foreigner, tke Eoglish farmer to a large extent become the manufacturer as well as consumer of the bricks, tiles, and pipes which he requires on his land. And one benefit resulting from this may be seen in the increased employment of labour in this branch of industry. Mr. Whitehead, of Preston, has acquired some degree of eminence as a maker of drain-pipe and tile machines, and shows a specimen or two which seem admirably adapted for these purposes. One of them is the tile prize machine to which was adjudged the premium of 20/. at the , Royal Agricultural Society's meeting at York, in 1848, and again at Norwich, in 1849 The box of this machine is capable of containing l cwt. of clay, and once filling enables it to throw out 55 two-inch, or 90 one and a half-inch tiles. The front of the box is .composed of a moveable die-plate, through which the clay is forced, in the form of pipes ' or tiles, on to a receiving table of rollers, where they are cut into any required lengths by iron wires, the action of which is the same as that of a saw, cutting the edges parfectly even and smooth, and performing the work in an instantaneous manner. One man may turn the machine and I supply the box the whole day, whilst a boy cuts the tiles or pipes and carries them away. Another tile-machine belonging to Mr. Whitehead has a double action, and may be used for making tiles or pipes, or pressing clay through a screen at either or both ends. By the former of these useful articles, at a trial at the Exeter meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society in 1850, one man and a boy made 520 two-inch tiles in ten minutes, and by the latter 724 two-inch I tiles in the same period. Of course the diameter of the pipe or the size of the tile varies according to the capacity of the ! die-plate. I Messrs. Smith of Stamford, exhibit a most efficient haymaking machine, an implement in the production of which they have made themselves famous. One horse is sufficient I to draw it through the hayfield, and the driver has never any occasion to quit the side of the horse, as he can instantly I and with ease elevate or depress the machine to the requisite I height. It has a reverse and double action, and the judges I of the Royal Agricultural Society, at the show at Norwich, in awarding the prize to its inventors, declared that it was so near perfection, that no man need fear buying, under the I impression that any great improvement would take place in lit in future." Subsequent experience has, however, suggested the substitution of wrought for cast iron, by which I means there are secured an increase of strength and durability, and a considerable lightening of the draught. To us it is not the best recommendation of this machine that it has done the work of tweety labourers at one time in a field. We have frequently seen it in operation, and the rapidity and effectiveness with which it does its work were certainly astonishing. THE GREAT EXHIBITION. :rhe building on Saturday was, as usual, quiet, select, and anstocratie. There was none Of the hurrying and excitel •Crowds that indicate the elms resolved and compelled to make the most of their time; but, on the contrary, numerous 'groups of laughing and chatting fashionables, discussing ' , everything but the Exhibition they had come to see, and: looking at none of the wonders it contained, but themselves. Nevertheless, it is evident that a change is gradually creeping - over the aspect of affairs, even on the Satarcley ; there is less asaunteeing in the transept and naves, an Mere guide-books 'and catalogues in requisition. Those who have gazed their till at its most striking features are now betaking themselves to the studyand explore" ion of its details, and in every out of the Way quarter of the building parties may be met with analysiug, discussing, and investigating, who have probably spent Weeks previously without ever travailing out of the main avenues. The Saturday visitors include the invalids,; who are afraid to encounter the crowd and pressure ; the early Dart of the week. We observed bath chairs in every direction, and among them a very ingenious con- Invance occupied by an invalid naval officer, who by a slight triFitien of the hand turning a horizontal wheel connected wiait what may be called the driving wheel of the chair )empels himself, without apparent effort, in any direction. tn dependently of the numerous piasioforte players . who are displaying their powers in different parts of the building the organs now supply the visitors with a series of musical entertainments of a high order. That of Messrs. Gray and Davidson at the east end at one period of the day; Dueroduet's French organ at another, and Willis's large organ at the west end at a further interval. Our only regret is that this large and powerful organ has not been earlier rendered available. The rivalry among the Exhibition painters is now become rather prominent. Nash, who exhibits three 'very beautifully coloured viewslif the interior, has taken up his quarters in Turkey, Where a person is in attendance to receive subscribers' names. On the opposite side of the nave, 'n China, Mr. Selous announces the attractions of his great historical picture of the inauguration of the building. And on the opposite side of the transept, on the borders of India, hovers the representative of Mr. Baxter, the inventor and patentee of oil-colour printing, who is bushy emeployed making sketches of the interior. The point upon he was engaged on Saturday was the opposite angle `of t4te Indian department, in which is displayed what may considered one of the curiosities of that distant empire. it is the dress of a Nautch, or dancing girl, of white muslin, measuring, if our lady readers will credit us, 291 yards in I circumference I Beside this is exhibited the petticoat of a Ber,ura, or Indian princess, not quite an capacious in its dimensions, but snaking up in the richness of the colours and gold embroidery for its apparently lesser amplitude. While on the subject of foreign curiosities, we may mention that among a number of wood, hot-n, bone, ivory, and other descriptions of spoons, arranged in a glass.case in the Turkish department, will be found two spoons, made of the beak of the spoon-bill heron, a bird now nearly extinct. These spoons are estimated so highly, that they are only =used by the Pacha ; they have beautifully carved coral handles, mounted in silver, and on the stem of each a large ruby. Theit rarity may be estimated when we state that the pair are valued at 70/. A curiosity of a very different description has been placed 'by Mr. Green, the ship-builder, of Blackwell, in the transept, beside the model of the Queen, 116 gnn•shin. It conmats of two pieces of stout sail-cloth cut from this maintop. sail of the ship Trafalgar, which encountered a severe hurricane off the Isle of France on the 21st of March last. The vessel was hove to under close-reefed fore and maintopsails, both of which were torn from the yards to shreds by the force of the wind. There is nothing extraordinary, of course, in stout new sails being so torn and rent by the wind, but the singularity in this case is that the strips of the sails are knotted in the firmest and most intricate manner, as if by some powerful machinery, and in a way that no ingenuity or force could undo. In addition to the abundant supply of water offered to the Visitors, a Mr. Perkins, the inventor of the hot-water oven, on Saturday presented them with a huge loaf weighing 38113., baked by his patented process. At a later period the art of coating and cameo cutting was discovered; and the celebrated Barberini vase, which has so long delighted artists and puzzled the dilettanti has turned out to be, not the work of the potter, but of the glass-blower and cutter. Tne Naples museum proves that the ltrthrions people who inhabited the cities overwhelmed by the eruptions of Vesuvius were well acvaint6S With the art; and among the Venetians the glassmeeer held a dignified position—the island of Murano, in one of the lagoons, being celebrated for its productions. One of the properties said to be possessed by the Venetian was that of flying to pieces when poison was intro. duced—a convenient myth which it was the interest of the nobles to impress upon the people. It is generily supposed that glee' making was introduced into Venice by the Crnsadere in the beginning of the 13th century. and for a long period it formed a lucrative commercial monopoly. Its perfection, however, was more comparative than real. We have still numerous specimens of what was considered the finest Venetian glass, and some of our manufacturers have succeeded in re-producing the fragile and delicate cups and vases of frosted and gilt Venetian glass, which was at one time considered almost priceless. The small band of Lotreines who were driven from their own country by civil dissensions and religious persecuion to take refuge in England, like the stout Flemings, to whom we owe another branch of mantifactitres, not finding encouragement in London, settled near Stourbridge, having observed there evidences of the invaluable fire-clay, out of which the glass melting-pots are formed.
