THE GREAT EXHIBITION. The opening of the great industrial entertainment, to which we have invited the people of all nations, having been appropriately and happily consummated by the Sovereign, surrounded by all the insignia of her pomp and power (her Majesty having in the name of the people of this country welcomed the myriad strangers from all climes who are now daily arriving on our shores), the most serious of the many difficulties which beset the labours of the Royal Commissioners having been overcome, and the whole world at liberty, we wish we could say "free," to wander through its vast expanse, and gaze upon the many marvels it contains, we propose proceeding upon a more systematic and detailed plan than we have hitherto adopted in our cursory glances over the general arrangements, and, by a reference to the most striking and important objects in the Exhibition of each country, point out the novelties, the contrasts, the improvements, or the defects which appear to us most obvious, and by this means render it to the people of this country, what his Roy al Highness expressed a hope it might prove, "a true test and living picture of the point of development at which the whole of mankind has arrived in the great task, and a new starting point from which all nations will be able to direct their further exertions." Our examination will be therefore mainly directed to pointing out the progresei made by the industry and the intellect of man in rendering subservient, and moulding and fashioning to his use, the raw material which the various departments of nature offer to him, and to trace the gradual improvements and developments which the lights of science, the aids of a higher and more cultivated taste, and a nicer appreciation of the beautiful in form, have effected within the last few years. The various contributions of the animal, the vegetable, and the mineral kingdom which are here exhibited, both in the state of raw material and in the matured productions of human thought and ingenuity, have been comprehended under a general arrangement, which, commencing with the the five great sections of raw materials and processesmachinery—manufactures, and fine arts are afterwards subdivided into 30 classes. This arrangement has been carried out as far as practicable in the British, the colonial, and the foreign departments of the Exhibition, and although, for all scientific and really practical purposes, this is the proper and legitimate division, the general visitor, while keeping this classification in view, will be able much more satisfactorily to make a survey of the contents of the Crystal Palace, and avoid much of its perplexities and intricacies, by examining the productions of each country separately. We propose in our present and succeeding notices to assist him in this plan by glancing at the productions of each in the order in which they are arranged in the Exhibition. The greater state of forwardness and more numerous and varied display of the western or British end of the Exhibition has rendered it, up to this time, the leading point of attraction; but if the show made by our foreign friends and rivals is not:so great, there are many points of excellence and many valuable suggestions which, we trust, will not be thrown away upon the artisans and manufacturers of this country. With the view of making the Exhibition in this way practically useful, and as a compliment to which the foreign contributors are fairly entitled, we shall commence with the extreme eastern point of the building, and proceed gradually down the nave to the other extremity, making occasional discursive visits to the cross-avenues and galleries, and in this way place our readers in a position to comprehend the general plan and features and the leading characteristics of each department. The United States department, which occupies the extreme east section of the Crystal Palace, challenges, when compared with others,; but little opportunity for remark. All those products of a high state of civilisation which we find in most of the European divisions are absent here, and the American exhibition, in this respect, fails to command that attention which is elicited in the more immediate neighbourhoods of France, Belgium, and Austria. The only two works belonging absolutely to the domains of fine art are Power's statue of the Greek slave, and Stephenson's statue of the wounded Indian. The former is well known in this country, where it has for a long time time been located in a private collection. The latter possesses a vast deal of merit, going far to prove that America will not long remain behind-hand in these msthetic efforts which betray more than anything else the influence of education, the progress of taste, and the refinements that flow from the intercoune with Europe. The expression of agony depicted in the face of the dying Indian is admirably conveyed, and the whole composition is fraught with character and intelligence. Situated also in the nave, and in close proximity to the two figures to which we have alluded, is a huge railway bridge, the specialty of which we cannot at present determine, for as yet it is many removes from corapletion. the north side of the nave, the chambers in the occupation of the United States are principally devoted to machinery and agricultural implements, the latter predominating. We have ploughs, grindstones, oil-cake-breakers, barrows, and the like, intermingled with tools of various kinds used for gardening and domestic purposes, none of them inviting any particular notice on the score of originality, though all exhibiting excellent and superior workmanship the mechanical details. On this side a large variety of stoves, ranges, and other apparatus of the same household class is alas to be seen, among which a calorie engine of a peculiar construction for heating and cooling air is one of the most prominent objects. A set of punching machines also attract the observation of the spectator, which, furnished with rolling or knuckle joints, the long levers of which pass through a space of many feet, and move over not more than half an inch, concentrate a large amount of power. Some safes of professedly equal security to those of Chubb's, and several other iron works, both cast and wrought, for cognate purposes, are placed in this department; and though of little interest in themselves, are undoubted attestations that all conveniences of this kind are manufactured with equal skill on the other side af the Atlantic as here. The illustrations of the India-rubber manufacture are numerous, including a life-boat, which, although 6 feet long and 3 feet wide, can be put into a person's pocket. Maps printed on calico, artificial legs and other specimens of mechanical surgery, paper-hangings, and various specimens of block printing as diverse in design as in colour, make up the remaining contents of leading prominence on the northern aide of this section ; though we must not forget to mention the show of carriages, and other vehicles of the same sort, which exhibit abundant ingenuity in the application of the mechanical principles the best sailed to ensure locomotive case, and the least possible expenditure of wear and tear. Crossing the nave and entering the southern division a vast profusion of daguerreotypes and calotypes arc to be seen These are of varices degrees if merits. Some ot them ale effective, but in no instance no tie observe anything superior. to what we are in the habit of witnessing daily at home. Some portraits executed by Bredy of New York are remarkable for their increased superficies in comparison with those to which we are accustomed, but the reflctant quality of the polished metal is necessarily augmented, and hence no advantage is gained. This gallery of daguerreotypes is chiefly curious on account of its portraiture of the most illustrious men of the United Stated. Calhoun and others are here in al their reality of aspect, and the spectator acquires an idea of the lineamente of many an individual distinguished for his talents and inflnence, for his power as an orator or his wisdom as a legislator, which it is clear any of the ordinary modes of limning fail to supply. Some of the talbotypes are bold and effective; and in this department of the photogenic art the Americans may be said to have surpassed us. There is a large asssrtment of popular optical instruments, including some'clever hyalotypes, or positive pictures on glass plates, adapted for magic lantern slides. The lithographs, which are exhibited in tolerable numbers, do not evince any gret proficiency in this branch of artistic manipulation. The drawing is, in most cmcs, poor, mechanical, and spiritless, and the lithographic texture coarse and woolly. Several of the portraits which we observe in the gallery of daguerrotypes are re-produced on stone; but, for the reasons we have stated, demand but little admiration. Pirsson, of New York, furnishes a pianoforte, adjusted for two performers, one at each end, which cupplies a want that has occasionally been felt ; at the same tone an economy of space, is secured worthy of consideration. The shape of the instrument is a parallelogram—in fact that of two grand pianofortes placed, invertedly, side by side; the actions being totally distinct. This, as well as a patent square pianoforte, are contained in finely embossed rosewood cases, and are very beautiful pieces of furniture. 01 the tone it is impossible to speak, for in such an area as that of the Crystal Palace any musical sound generated by a process so delicate must inevitably be shorn of any resonance :and beauty which it may possess. Another pianoforte, from the factory of Meyer, of Philadelphia, is constructed almost wholly of iron frames, in which respect it bears some affinity to the euphonicon, which, a year or two ago, was patented in this country by the eminent firm of Beale and Co., the only difference being in the shape. Other musical instruments figure in pro' fusion, but they are simply the contents of an ordinary music-shop. At the extreme east of this side there is a large display of glass-rare, as well a fine model of a glass factory and all that appertains to it. The textile fabrics of the United States are exhibited in an imposing manner. The printed cottons from New York and Massachusetts evidence the growing skill of the Americans, not only in the conception of pattern, but in the superiority of manufacture and the flannels, blankets, and cassimeres, &c., from the same districts, here displayed, are, in short, most favourable examples of American industry, and, as such, merit examination. The furrier trade is also well exemplified; so likewise boot and shoe-making, book-binding, and divers other handicrafts. Scientific instruments are to be found in great abundance, besides entire chemical laboratories. Several specimens of oil-cloth also appear on this side of the nave, whose brilliancy and decision of colour at once strike and gratify the eye. But it is in the raw materials of the country that the chief interest of the American exhibition mainly rests. There is a large collection of woods and vegetable substances from Maryland, arranged in a spacious cabinet. It will easily be supposed that metallic ores are no less plentiful. Ohio sends a large assortment of geological specimens, and it has been well and truthfully remarked, that, on looking at them, "No one can avoid the thought that the district producing such minerals must possess a most valuable mine upon which industry has only to exercise her skill." The specimens of vegetable produce include tobacco, Genessee flour, Indian corn, and malt prepared from it, maple sugar, mustard, oil of peppermint, and the like, to which we can only incidentally refer, but which will repay examination. The gallery in the occupation of our Transatlantic brethren is at present but scantily filled, the chief tenant being a perfumer from Philadelphia, who seems to pride himself upon his fancy soaps, some of which he has moulded into busts and other configurations. Such are the principal contents of the space allotted to the United States. At the first glance, the objects, we repeat, are not so striking as those of a showier and more ornamental kind, but still there is much that is worthy of scrutiny, much to amuse, much to instruct. The want of a catalogue by which the various articles may be identified, and their points of interest elucidated, is at present sorely felt, for though the sixpenny synopsis which is officially published gives a pleasant insight into the class of things to be observed, it does not contain a syllable of detail. This, it is to be hoped, will be remedied in a few days, when the doors of the Palace are shut against further contributions, and the Exhibition is pronounced complete. Russia, to whom a very extensive hay or compartment has beea allotted in the north of the nave, and a smaller one in the south, comes next in point of locality, and we are sorry to find that her real geographical position has been the means of leaving the greater part of the space allotted to her by the Royal Commissioners up to the present time a waste as barren and deserted as one of her own steppes. The vessel freighted to convey the great bulls of her goods to the Exhibition was for several weeks frozen up in the ice, and it will, we understand, be some weeks yet before the goods will all be landed and fully displayed. There are a few very beautiful articles displayed, which make us only the more anxious to see the industrial resources of this vast empire fully developed. In front of the compartment are two massive richly chased and gilt candelabra, about ten feet high, standing on triangular pedestals of black marble; they are very fine examples of parqueterie, and the finish and proaortions are faultless. Some jasper eases, well finished and highly polished, exhibit novelty of design, and there are two very large porcelain vases enriched with raised vine leaves and stems in dead gold. The enamel paintings on these vases are very delicately executed. A circular table in metal, with the painting on the slab annealed, has no pretensions to artistic merit. There are a Large number of electrotype and plastic medallions and casts, bat the most striking and elaborate contribution at present displayed is a cabinet in tulip wood, ornamented with bronze and porcelain. The medallions on the panels are very fine specimens of painting, and the whole is extremely creditable to the St. Petersburgh manufacturer. Two grand pianos in rosewood are plain substantial looking instraments, possessing little of the finish or decoration of the French or English workshops. A table inlaid with various stones in Florentine mosaic, and mounted on an elaborately carved bronze gilt pillar, and some specimens of coloured inlaid floors, comprise nearly all the articles in the northern compartment, and the southern portion is still less furnished. One of the curiosities exhibited is a miniature likeness of the to represent a fine steel engraving, which turns out to be executed in black needlework upon a white ground. In the centre of the compartment of Sweden and Norway is a marble statue of a shepherd's boy, executed at Rome by M. Moline, a Swedish sculptor, possessing considerable merit. As might naturally be anticipated, these countries are rich in illustrations of the manufacture of metal. There are various specimens of ore from the mines of Bofors and Dannemora, and a large number of tubes, iron plates, files, cutlery, inlaid with gold and silver, sabres and daggers, if they do not present the same finish as our own articles, show the high temper and superior character of the Swedish steel. Cotton and woollen goods, of coarse bat substantial texture, produced in the hand looms of the peasantry, and Swedish silks and satins, moire faconnee, and a portrait of King Oscar, woven in silk by the Jacquard loom, are among the textile fabrics exhibited. There are also specimens of cobalt and nickel from the Norwegian mines. The whole of this little collection is extremely interesting. Danmark stands next in geographical position, and shows many curious mechanical contrivancss, which display a good dell of ingenuity. There is a modification of the machine, introduced some years ago in this c ,untry, for composing and adjusting types, which it is said obviates many of the objections of the original. A pump, which can be converted into a steam-gauges, astronomical clocks, self-registering thermometers,ezimuths,&c. There arc a large number of contributions from the Royal porcelain manufactory at Copenhagen, which are very delicately executed. Much of the business of this establishment of late years has been devoted to producing reduced copies of the works of the celebrated sculptor Thorswaldsen, in bisque china, and most of them are here, as well as has reliefs in biscuit, of sacred, allegoricel, and mythological subjects. HIGHLAND JEWELLERY.-ThIe seasons 1849 and 1S50 were remarkable to the seekers of precious stones in the Cairomorm range of mountains, for the abundance with which the genius of the hills gave up his treasures. It was supposed, and possibly with truth, that the unusual plenty of the beautiful crystals was attributable to the unprecedented character of the floods which marked tihe opening of the first named of those years-sweeping clown, as the angry waters did, vast quantities of earth and rock from the higher and less accessible parts of the mountains, and clear- ing out many a spot where the stones had been hidden for scores of years. The search, as we mentioned some time ego, was resumed this season with some little spirit, though the number of searchers was not so great as in the two preceding summers; but, so far as we can learn, no great good fortuio has attended the season hunting. Few might have been the crystals brought into the town for sale-we might rather say none; and fortunate it was for the jewellers that the stocks they laid in during the preceding plenty, were large enough to carry them through the scarcity now experienced. The popularity of Cairn- germ bijouterie seems to be much on the increase, and certainly the beauty and variety of the ornaments in which it is used with effect, and the really lovely shades of some of the crystals, are good reasons why they should come Into general favour. The other day we were shown a brooch, the stone of which, and a large one it was, might almost have passed for a monster ruby, so brilliant and so ruddy were its sparkling hues.
